section: 0.1 Forecasting and Warning Data and Digital Asset Governance
text:
0.1 Forecasting and Warning Data and Digital Asset Governance
The Forecasting and Warning team operates a complex set of flood models, data pipelines, and code tools that collectively underpin operational Flood Incident Management. As the team and its technical environment have grown, a clear gap has emerged: there is no consistent, documented framework governing how these assets are built, managed, or handed over.
This has practical consequences. Models are updated without version records. Code tools lack owners, documentation, or tests. Hydrometric data enters pipelines without a traceable audit trail. When a team member leaves or moves on, knowledge leaves with them. When a tool fails, there is no standard process for understanding what went wrong or how to fix it.
The absence of governance also creates a compliance risk. The team’s assets and outputs are used to inform real decisions during flood events. Without documented quality standards, provenance tracking, and role accountability, it is difficult to demonstrate that those outputs are fit for purpose.
This work establishes a governance framework to address these gaps. It sets out clear roles and responsibilities, defines quality standards for data and models, and establishes proportionate rules for code development and tool promotion. The aim is not to add bureaucracy, but to give the team a shared foundation: one that supports reproducible outputs, safe handovers, and confident operational delivery.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.1 Purpose
This framework sets out how the Forecasting and Warning (F&W) department manages its data, code, and digital assets. It defines who is responsible for what, at every level, covering all assets from strategic accountability for major datasets down to day-to-day maintenance of individual code tools.
The framework operates at two levels. This document covers governance principles, roles, and standards that apply to all assets regardless of type. Companion documents cover detailed code-level guidance for tools written in each language. Where those documents are silent, this framework takes precedence. This framework does not replace or supersede existing technical guidance, such as the RTMDG, it is a guide to how we manage assets not construct them.
The Owner, Steward, and Custodian roles used throughout this framework are defined in the Data Ownership Model and Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO) roadmap 2022 to 2025, which is the top-level authority for data ownership roles and responsibilities across government. This framework applies those roles to the specific assets and working practices of the F&W team.
This work also directly supports the team’s obligations under Defra’s Q-FAIR data standards aims. Q-FAIR requires that data assets are of sufficient Quality to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. Rather than treating Q-FAIR compliance as a separate reporting exercise, this framework and its companion documents build it in by design. Structured asset registers make data and tools findable. Consistent file formats and schemas make them interoperable and reusable. Defined access controls and storage locations make them accessible. The tier-based quality gates and quality flags directly address the Quality dimension. Compliance is therefore a natural outcome of following the framework, not additional work on top of it.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.3 Governance Roles
The team uses an Owner, Steward, and Custodian model as defined in the government Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2024). Each role has a defined grade, clear responsibilities, and can be formally delegated. These roles apply to all asset types covered by this framework, including model files, datasets, and code tools.

2.3.1 Owner (Deputy Director)
The Owner is a senior individual with dedicated accountability for a logical grouping of data or assets and in-depth knowledge of the overall business strategy in their area. Owners hold ultimate accountability for meaning, content, quality, and distribution of their assets. They make strategic decisions about how assets are used, shared, or retired. There is one Owner per major asset or tool.






Owner Grade Requirement



The CDDO Data Ownership Model recommends that Data Owners should be senior individuals but does not mandate a specific grade. The Defra Data Ownership Policy recommends SCS level. This framework requires Deputy Director grade for all Owners. This is an intentional local requirement under internal Defra group guidance and reflects the operational significance of the team’s assets to Flood Incident Management.


Owners are responsible for:

Approving what data and models the team uses and produces
Deciding who can access sensitive or nationally significant outputs
Signing off on major changes to modelling approach, data standards, or tool promotion to Tier 1
Resolving escalated disputes about data quality, access, or tool governance
Ensuring the team meets organisational data governance obligations
Understanding how assets are being used, who by, and whether they are controlled properly
Ensuring appropriate retention schedules are in place for all data
Ensuring their data assets comply with legal requirements for archival, disposal, and preservation
Limiting access to data (particularly personal data or data of significance to national security) to those authorised to do so
Ensuring security measures are in place to protect data in transit, received, or transferred to another organisation
Considering where data assets may have value to wider government, society, and the economy, and the protection and exploitation approaches required to realise that value (see Section 2.13)



2.3.2 Steward (Grade 7)
The Steward is responsible for day-to-day operational activities needed to support governance decisions made by Owners. Stewards are the operational points of contact with data expertise. They make sure standards are followed and assets are fit for purpose. Each asset or tool should have a named Steward.
Stewards are responsible for:

Defining and maintaining data standards, naming conventions, and quality requirements
Keeping asset registers and Tool Registers up to date
Reviewing model quality, version control, and metadata completeness
Approving access requests and code tool promotion between tiers
Coordinating with Custodians to ensure good practice
Reporting data quality issues or risks to the Owner
Handling data governance queries and checking with the Owner for tactical guidance where needed
Reviewing and updating this framework and the companion documents as part of annual updates
Maintaining a data catalogue or business glossary of centralised data definitions for all assets within their domain, ensuring definitions are managed and adopted consistently across the team (see Section 2.8)
Understanding data lineage and flow: knowing how data moves through pipelines, what transformations are applied, and the upstream and downstream impacts of any change
Managing the data lifecycle for assets within their domain, including archival, retention review, and coordinating disposal where retention periods have expired and Owner approval has been obtained
Working cross-functionally with stewards in adjacent teams or domains, sharing good practice and supporting resolution of cross-cutting data issues
Assisting with periodic data maturity assessments as required by the organisation
Periodically considering whether team data assets have value to wider government, society, or the economy, and flagging opportunities to the Owner (see Section 2.13)

Not all of these responsibilities carry equal weight at every tier. For Tier 3 assets, the core requirements are standards maintenance, register currency, and quality issue reporting. The fuller responsibilities (data lineage mapping, cross-functional liaison, maturity assessments, and wider value consideration) apply in proportion to asset criticality. All apply in full to Tier 1 assets.


2.3.3 Custodian (Any Grade)
The Custodian is responsible for capturing, storing, maintaining, and (where applicable) disposing of data and digital assets in line with the Owner’s requirements. Custodians do the hands-on work: creating, running, storing, and maintaining assets correctly. They work closely with Stewards to ensure quality by executing within agreed systems according to rules and standards. Any team member can be a Custodian.






Custodian Disposal Responsibility



The CDDO Data Ownership Model and Defra Data Ownership Policy both define the Custodian as responsible for “capturing, storing and disposing of data.” The majority of data held by the F&W team is observed environmental data (river flows, rainfall, water levels) which is generally retained indefinitely as it cannot be recreated and has enduring scientific and audit value. However, the disposal responsibility is included here to cover assets where retention limits do apply: superseded configuration files, deprecated tool artefacts, or data received under licence terms that include a disposal obligation. Disposal of any data requires Owner approval and must be documented.


Custodians are responsible for:

Following naming conventions, folder structures, and coding standards set by Stewards
Using version control correctly
Recording model run settings, tool configurations, and any issues encountered
Flagging data quality problems or tool failures to their Steward promptly
Not sharing assets outside agreed channels without permission
Spotting and reporting data governance issues to the Steward
Carrying out disposal of data or digital assets when directed by the Owner and Steward, and documenting the disposal decision, date, method, and authorisation
Ensuring that changes to data content and controls can be audited



2.3.4 Role Summary







Role
Definition and Responsibilities




Owner
Senior individual with ultimate accountability for a data or asset domain. Sets strategic direction, approves major decisions, ensures compliance. Deputy Director grade required (see note above). May be delegated to another Deputy Director or equivalent.


Steward
Operational expert responsible for day-to-day governance. Maintains standards, reviews quality, manages access, oversees the Tool Register and data catalogue, handles governance queries, tracks data lineage, manages lifecycle. Grade 7 required for Tier 1 tools; Grade 7 recommended for all other assets. Where the Steward’s strength is oversight and people management rather than technical depth, a Delegated Steward should be named to carry out the hands-on governance work: code quality assessment, model condition reviews, data pipeline evaluation, and the annual Tier 1 audit. Typically G6 grade.


Custodian
Technical expert responsible for capturing, storing, maintaining, and disposing of assets correctly. Creates, stores, and maintains assets and tools to agreed standards. Carries out disposal when authorised. Any grade. May be delegated to any team member.





2.3.5 Delegation
Any role may be formally delegated. Delegation must be:

Agreed between the delegating person and the delegate
Recorded in the relevant register with a start date and end date (or noted as ongoing)
Reviewed periodically or annually

Delegation does not transfer accountability. The original role holder remains responsible even when a role has been delegated.


2.3.6 Relationship to the Information Asset Owner Role
The Cabinet Office IAO guidance (updated October 2025) and the Defra Data Ownership Policy both recognise the Information Asset Owner (IAO) as a distinct role focused on the security, content, quality, and distribution of information assets. The CDDO Data Ownership Model notes that organisations may wish to combine the Data Owner and IAO roles where appropriate.
Within the F&W team, the Data Owner fulfils the IAO function for the team’s asset domain. The Deputy Director who holds the Owner role is accountable for the information assets (databases, data stores, model repositories) that contain the team’s data, as well as for the data itself. This combined accountability is appropriate given the team’s structure: the same individual needs oversight of both the logical data groupings and the systems that hold them.
Where the team’s data assets are held within wider organisational information assets (for example, data held within a shared Databricks environment or a centrally managed file store), the team’s Data Owner coordinates with the organisational IAO for that system to ensure that access controls, security measures, and risk assessments are aligned.
The Steward acts as the operational equivalent of an Information Asset Manager (IAM), carrying out the day-to-day management responsibilities on behalf of the Owner/IAO.
The following accountabilities from the IAO guidance are explicitly held by the team’s Data Owner:

Understanding what information is held within the team’s area of responsibility
Reviewing risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information assets
Ensuring information is appropriately protected and marked
Inputting into the departmental information asset register
Ensuring compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, UK GDPR, FOI and EIR regulations, and the Public Records Act
Ensuring that any AI service has been assessed before it is allowed access to team information assets (see Section 2.14)

2.5 The Tier System
Not all assets carry the same risk. A script that broke at 2am during a live flood event is a different problem to one that broke during a research exercise the following week. The tier system exists to make that difference explicit, and to calibrate the governance overhead accordingly.
All team assets, whether data, models, or code tools, are classified into one of three tiers based on their role in live operational forecasting. Tier 1 is operational: failure has direct consequences for the service. Tier 2 is analytical: regularly used, but not in the critical path. Tier 3 is experimental: research or prototype work, not in production. The tier determines the level of oversight required. It does not describe quality or maturity in isolation; a technically excellent piece of work begins at Tier 3 until its governance is confirmed.
The same three tiers apply to every asset type. That uniformity is deliberate. It gives the team a shared language for risk, regardless of whether the asset in question is a hydrometric dataset, a hydraulic model, or a Python script.










Tier
Description
Data
Models
Tools




Tier 1: Operational
Used in live forecasting. Failure has direct operational consequences.
Formally approved datasets feeding live model runs or supporting the service
FMP, PDM, Black Box and Boundary Conditions used in the operational forecast chain
Scripts and pipelines running in live forecasting or critical to supporting the service


Tier 2: Analytical
Regularly used but not in the critical forecasting path.
Calibration inputs, validated datasets used for post-event analysis
Models under active development or used for post-event analysis
Visualisation tools, performance dashboards, model comparison tools


Tier 3: Experimental
Research or prototype stage. Not in production.
Exploratory datasets, preliminary ingestion, unvalidated inputs
New model configurations being calibrated or tested
Research notebooks, proof-of-concept tools, ML experiments



Promotion to Tier 1 requires Owner sign-off for all asset types. Demotion or deprecation requires Owner approval. Assets begin at Tier 3 and are promoted as their maturity and governance are confirmed. An asset must not be used in live forecasting until it has been formally promoted to Tier 1.

2.5.1 Data Tiers and the Medallion Architecture
Hydrometric data arrives from many sources and rarely arrives clean. A gauge record from the Environment Agency’s API and a manually submitted spreadsheet from a partner organisation are both raw data, but they carry different levels of trust, different provenance trails, and different likelihoods of containing errors. Treating them identically at ingestion, or leaving quality decisions implicit, creates problems that compound downstream.
The medallion architecture addresses this by making quality stages explicit. Bronze is the unmodified record of what was received. Silver is the result of documented quality control. Gold is a formally approved product derived from Silver and cleared for a specific operational use. Each stage represents a distinct level of accountability. Moving data from one stage to the next requires deliberate action and a recorded decision. That is not bureaucracy; it is how the team knows what it is working with.
The medallion and the operational tier system answer different questions. The tier system asks: how critical is this asset to the live service? The medallion asks: how far has this data been through quality assurance? For code tools and models these two dimensions tend to move together. For hydrometric data they are genuinely independent, and that independence matters. The same Silver dataset might supply a Tier 2 post-event analysis today and a Tier 1 operational model run next month. The data’s quality state has not changed; only its use has. Conflating the two frameworks would mean re-approving data every time its purpose changed.
The medallion architecture is not optional. Only Gold-tier data may be used as input to Tier 1 model runs or ML model training that may one day be promoted to operational use. See Chapter 5 for the full schema requirements and QC process.


2.5.2 Model Tiers
Flood models, including FMP hydraulic models, PDM rainfall-runoff configurations, boundary conditions, and Black Box elements, are classified under the same three-tier system. A model’s tier reflects its role in the operational forecast chain, not its technical sophistication. See Chapter 6 for full details.


2.5.3 Tool Tiers
Code tools written in R or Python follow the same tier system. A tool’s tier reflects the operational consequences of failure. Tier 1 tools require the most rigorous development, testing, and custodianship standards. See Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 for language-specific requirements.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.6 Flood Model Governance
FMP model files require formal version control because they contain binary and configuration files that change with every calibration update, boundary condition revision, or software upgrade. Both the current model and all superseded versions must be retained. A model that produced a formal output must remain recoverable in the exact state it was in when that output was produced. No FMP files may be held on local machines or unmanaged drives.
PDM parameter sets, calibration records, and coupled model configurations follow the same governance principles. Parameter sets are particularly sensitive: a set calibrated on one period of data can produce materially different outputs from a set calibrated on a different period, even for the same catchment. Version control and calibration documentation are not optional.
The detailed requirements for folder structure, naming conventions, version control, run records, condition assessment, and model connections are set out in the Flood Model Governance document (Chapter 6). The requirements there are normative and must be followed by all Custodians working with operational models.

text:
2.7 Code and Tool Governance
The department currently develops and maintains code tools in R and Python. These tools are governed by the same Owner, Steward, and Custodian framework as all other assets, with additional requirements that reflect the specific risks of code: unreproducible results, undocumented behaviour, and key-person dependency.
This section sets out the governance principles that apply to all code tools regardless of language. Detailed, language-specific standards are in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4.

2.7.1 Tool Classification
All code tools are classified into one of three tiers based on their operational role. Governance requirements increase with tier level.








Tier
Description
Examples




Tier 1: Operational
Used in live forecasting; failure has direct operational consequences
Ensemble processing scripts, alert threshold tools, Flood Modeller API orchestration, operational ML inference pipelines


Tier 2: Analytical
Regularly used but not in the critical forecasting path
Visualisation tools, performance metrics dashboards, model comparison tools


Tier 3: Experimental
Research or prototype stage; not in production
New model evaluation scripts, proof-of-concept tools, ML experiments, research notebooks

Role
Tier 1: Operational
Tier 2 and 3: Analytical / Experimental




Owner
Deputy Director required. Must be a different individual from the Steward.
Deputy Director strongly recommended. A senior manager with equivalent accountability may be assigned where agreed with the Delegated Steward.

Grade 7 recommended. A capable team member at a lower grade may act as Steward for Tier 3 tools where the role is combined with Custodian.


Custodian
Runs scheduled CI checks, monitors for issues, escalates to Steward promptly, maintains disaster recovery runbook.
Runs tests before major language version upgrades, flags broken dependencies to Steward.



When a team member leaves or changes role, custodianship must be formally reassigned before their departure.


2.7.3 Routes to Tool Development
There are four routes by which a new tool enters the team’s codebase. The route must be agreed at the point of initiation and recorded in the Tool Register.








Route
Description
Typical Origin




A: New Standalone Tool
A new script or module developed from scratch. Begins at Tier 3 and may be promoted. Proposed via a Git issue; Steward confirms route and tier within five working days.
Identified gap in team capability; new forecasting requirement


B: Shared Module / Package Contribution
A function or class developed for inclusion in a shared package (Flode for R, shared module for Python). Follows a promotion pathway with API review by the Steward Lead.
Recurring code pattern across tools; refactoring of existing standalone tool


C: Adoption of External Package
An externally developed package being formally adopted for team use. Personal Tier 3 use is acceptable; shared or production use requires evaluation and sign-off.
Discovered package that meets a team need; tool shared by a partner organisation


D: Emergency / Hotfix
A tool or fix developed under time pressure. Verbal authorisation from the Steward required before work begins.
Forecasting failure; urgent fix required



For Route C, all external packages must be evaluated against six criteria before adoption in shared or production code: active maintenance, compatible licence, acceptable performance impact, manageable dependency footprint, genuine necessity, and sufficient community adoption.
For Route D, no more than two emergency route deployments per twelve-month period for the same tool area is acceptable before triggering a review of the underlying operational code tools.


2.7.4 Code Review Requirements







Tier
Review Requirement




Tier 1: Operational
Mandatory peer review by a second team member before merging to main. Senior reviewer sign-off before first production deployment. Annual audit of all Tier 1 tools.


Tier 2: Analytical
Peer review required before merging to main. Reviewer must have at least intermediate proficiency in the relevant language.


Tier 3: Experimental

2.7.5 Version Control Principles
All code tools used by more than one person must be managed in Git. No shared tool may exist solely on a local machine or shared drive.
Branching: the team follows a simplified Git Flow model: main (production-ready only, no direct commits), develop (integration branch), feature/<n> (individual work), hotfix/<n> (urgent fixes to Tier 1), release/<version> (versioned releases).
Commits: all commits must follow the Conventional Commits convention <type>(<scope>): <short description> with a body explaining why, not just what. Permitted types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore.
Versioning: all tools and packages follow Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Releases are tagged in Git and accompanied by a CHANGELOG.md entry.
Reproducibility: all dependencies must be pinned and committed alongside the code: renv.lock for R tools, poetry.lock for Python tools. Code must be runnable from a clean environment without undeclared dependencies.


2.7.6 Tool Register
Every code tool must be entered in the central Tool Register at the point it is shared with more than one team member. The register is a CSV file (tool_register.csv) held in this governance repository and generated by scripts/build_tool_register.R. It is not edited by hand.
The script works in two passes. First, it queries the GitHub API for all repositories in the JonPayneEA organisation and extracts the fields GitHub holds natively: repository name, URL, primary language, and topics. Second, for each repository it reads a governance.yml file from the repository root, which supplies the governance fields GitHub cannot know. Values in governance.yml take precedence over inferred values; GitHub topics are used as a fallback for tier and status.
A template governance.yml is provided in this repository at governance-template.yml. Every tool repository must include a populated copy in its root. Two GitHub topic conventions are required on every tool repository, and used as fallback when governance.yml is absent or incomplete:

Tier: one of tier-1, tier-2, tier-3
Status: one of active, under-development, deprecated

2.7.7 Handover and Succession
When a Steward or Custodian changes, the outgoing person must produce a handover note before they leave. The note covers: the tool’s purpose and known quirks, current technical debt or open issues, the status of any open pull requests, and scheduled maintenance tasks. It is stored in the tool’s docs/ directory.
For Tier 1 tools, the incoming Steward must run the full test suite and confirm it passes before formally accepting the handover. The Delegated Steward must be notified of all Tier 1 custodianship changes.

2.8 Data Catalogue and Centralised Definitions
The Steward is responsible for maintaining a data catalogue or business glossary that records centralised definitions for the team’s key data entities, attributes, and terminology. This aligns with the CDDO Data Ownership Model requirement that agreed data definitions be maintained through Data Stewards.
The data catalogue should cover at minimum:

Definitions for the team’s core data types (flow, stage, rainfall, catchment descriptors) and what each means in the team context
The relationship between supplier terminology and team terminology (for example, mapping supplier quality codes to the team’s flag scheme)
Definitions for key model parameters and what they represent physically
Naming conventions for datasets, tools, and models, consolidated from across the governance suite

The catalogue is maintained by the Steward and reviewed as part of the annual governance audit. It may take the form of a structured document, a spreadsheet, or a dedicated section within the team’s internal documentation site.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.11 Data Incidents and Escalation
A data incident is any event that affects the integrity, availability, or confidentiality of team assets including accidental deletion, use of wrong input data in a published output, tool failure in a live operational forecast environment, or unauthorised sharing.
When an incident occurs:

The Custodian reports it to the Steward immediately
All incidents are recorded in the governance log with a summary of what happened and what was done
The Steward escalates to the Owner immediately where the incident affects a formal output, an external stakeholder, or carries potential regulatory or reputational implications; for all other incidents, the Steward uses their judgement

For any Tier 1 asset failure or emergency deployment (Route D), a post-incident review must be completed within ten working days. The review covers: what happened, what the impact was or could have been, what was done to resolve it, and what change is needed to prevent recurrence. The Steward is responsible for completing the review and submitting it to the Owner.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.12 Monitoring, Reporting, and Risk Management
The CDDO Data Ownership Model requires that ownership policies include monitoring and reporting arrangements as part of the organisation’s broader risk management practices. The following cadence applies:
Quarterly: The Steward produces a governance summary covering: data quality trends from the Hydrometric Data Framework quarterly summaries, open Data Quality Issue Log entries and their age, Tool Register and Model Register currency, any incidents or near-misses in the quarter, and supplier engagement outcomes. This summary is shared with the Owner and feeds into the team’s quarterly governance review.
Annually: The Delegated Steward conducts a full governance audit of all Tier 1 assets (code tools, models, and data). Findings are compiled into an annual governance report, which is presented to the Owner and submitted to the organisational risk management process. The report covers: compliance rates across all Tier 1 assets, condition rating trends for models, test coverage and documentation currency for tools, data quality trends, and any governance exceptions granted during the year.
On occurrence: Data incidents, governance exceptions, and emergency deployments (Route D) are reported to the Steward immediately and to the Owner where they affect formal outputs. Patterns of recurring incidents or exceptions are flagged in the quarterly summary and, if persistent, escalated to the organisation’s risk register.
Non-compliance. Where the annual audit identifies assets that do not meet the requirements of this framework, the Delegated Steward produces a corrective action plan within one month of the audit report. The plan specifies the gap, the required action, the responsible Custodian or Steward, and a target date. Assets with outstanding corrective actions are flagged in the quarterly summary until resolved. Persistent or repeated non-compliance with Tier 1 requirements is escalated to the Owner and documented in the governance log. An asset that has failed to meet a corrective action target without documented justification must not be used in a new formal output until the gap is resolved.
The Owner is responsible for ensuring that governance findings are communicated to the broader organisational governance and risk management structures as appropriate.

2.13 Wider Data Value
The CDDO Data Ownership Model requires organisations to consider where data assets may have value to wider government, society, and the economy. The Steward should periodically (at least annually, as part of the governance review) consider whether any of the team’s data assets, particularly Gold-tier hydrometric data, model validation datasets, or calibration benchmarks, could have value to other Defra teams, other government departments, academic researchers, or the public.
Where an opportunity is identified, the Steward flags it to the Owner with a brief assessment of the data’s potential value, any licensing or access constraints, and any preparation work that would be needed. The Owner decides whether to pursue sharing, taking account of supplier licence terms, data sensitivity, and resource implications.
This does not create an obligation to share all data. It creates an obligation to ask the question.

title: 2  Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework
text:
2.14 AI and Machine Learning Governance
The team uses AI and ML tools in two ways: commercial or external services that may access team data, and internally developed ML models that feed operational forecasts. Both require governance. Neither is well-served by ad-hoc decisions.
Assessment before access. Before any AI or ML service is given access to team data, the Steward must assess three things: what data the service will access and at what tier, whether that data contains personal or sensitive information requiring a DPIA, and whether the service complies with government Secure by Design principles. The assessment is a short written record, approved by the Owner and stored alongside the relevant Tool Register entry or dataset provenance record. This applies equally to commercial tools (such as Microsoft Copilot or cloud inference APIs) and to internally developed inference pipelines.
ML models in operational use. Any ML model whose outputs feed Tier 1 forecasts is itself a Tier 1 asset. It must have a named Custodian, a training dataset recorded as a Gold product (see Chapter 5), version-controlled model artefacts with a JSON metadata file, and a formal condition assessment on the Tier 1 review schedule. The Python governance document (Chapter 4) sets out the technical requirements for training and inference separation, metadata files, and ONNX archiving.
Run record requirements. For any ML model used in an operational forecast, the run record must identify the model version, the training dataset version, and any known limitations. Where an ML model replaces a physically-based model, the replacement decision must be documented, comparative performance evidence provided, and the change approved by the Owner before deployment.
The Steward monitors developments in AI legislation and government guidance that affect the team’s use of ML tools. This is reviewed as part of the annual governance audit.

text:
2.15 Review and Compliance
This framework and the companion documents are reviewed annually by the Stewards (or subject matter experts), with Owner sign-off. The review considers:

Whether the asset categories and roles are still fit for purpose
Any incidents or near-misses from the previous year
Changes to tools, data sources, or organisational requirements
Feedback from Custodians on what is working and what is not
Alignment with any updates to the CDDO Data Ownership Model, Defra Data Ownership Policy, IAO guidance, or relevant legislation

The Delegated Steward conducts an annual audit of all Tier 1 code tools, covering header block completeness, test coverage, documentation currency, dependency lockfile consistency, and branching strategy compliance.
Stewards must carry out spot-check audits of Tier 2 model files and metadata records at least once per year, and of Tier 3 assets at least once every two years. Spot checks may be carried out at any time.

2.15.1 Framework Version Control
Changes to this document and the companion documents fall into three categories.
Editorial corrections are typos, broken links, or formatting fixes that do not change meaning. The Delegated Steward may make and merge editorial corrections at any time without Owner sign-off. No version increment. No team notification required, though the change is visible in the git history.
Substantive changes are anything that changes a requirement, adds or removes a role, adds or removes a process step, or modifies a companion document in a way that affects practice. Substantive changes require Owner sign-off before they are merged. The minor version number increments (1.4 becomes 1.5). The Steward notifies the team by written summary within five working days of the merge, identifying which sections changed and why.
Major changes are restructures of the tier system, redefinition of core roles, or changes that require existing registers to be migrated or existing assets to be re-assessed. Major changes trigger a full review cycle and increment the major version number (1.4 becomes 2.0). They are treated the same as a new framework adoption.
For all substantive and major changes, the procedure is:

Draft the change on a branch
Record the rationale in the Change Log in Appendix D before requesting sign-off
Obtain Owner sign-off
Merge and increment the version number in _quarto.yml (master) and in the metadata block of the changed document
Update the review dates in any companion documents that reference the changed section

The version field in _quarto.yml is the master. All companion document metadata blocks reference it and must be kept in step.

6.1 2.1 The Flode Package Ecosystem
All team R tools intended for reuse or sharing must be developed as components of or be compatible with Flode, the team’s overarching R package.






What is Flode? Flode is the team’s primary internal R package. Installing Flode gives users access to the full set of shared team functions. Individual sub-packages or modules can also be developed as standalone packages that Flode re-exports. All new reusable tools should be built with eventual inclusion in Flode in mind.






6.1.1 2.1.1 Flode Architecture
Flode is structured as a meta-package with functional sub-modules. New tools should be developed in the most appropriate module:






Module Names Under Review



The Flode module names listed below are provisional and subject to change. The team will confirm the final naming convention before the next version of this document. The module scopes are agreed; only the names may change.









Flode Module
Scope




reach.io
Data ingestion and export: reading gauge records, gridded rainfall, NWP outputs, and writing standardised forecast files


reach.hydro
Core hydrological calculations: flow statistics, unit conversions, catchment aggregation, flood frequency


reach.ensemble
Ensemble processing: member weighting, quantile extraction, probabilistic thresholding


reach.viz
Visualisation: standardised ggplot2-compatible chart themes and flood-specific plot functions


reach.validate
Model validation and skill scoring: bias metrics, skill scores, verification against observed records


reach.utils
General utilities: date/time helpers, path management, logging, configuration loading





6.1.2 2.1.2 Promoting Code into Flode
A function progresses from a standalone script into Flode through a defined pathway:

Developed as a Tier 3 tool with full header block and inline comments
Peer reviewed and tested to Tier 2 standard
Proposed to the Flode Steward via a GitHub issue with a brief rationale for inclusion
Reviewed against Flode’s API design consistency; refactored if needed
Full roxygen2 documentation written; tests achieving 70% coverage
Merged into the relevant Flode module by the Steward; exported in NAMESPACE
Version increment to Flode following Semantic Versioning

title: 3  R Tool Governance
text:
6.2 2.2 Coding Style and Conventions
All team R code follows a style guide tailored to the fastverse ecosystem. Where guidance is not provided below, defer to the data.table style conventions rather than tidyverse conventions.

6.2.1 2.2.1 Naming Conventions

Functions: snake_case verbs (e.g., calc_flood_peak(), load_gauge_dt())
data.table objects: suffix _dt to make the type explicit (e.g., flow_dt, ensemble_dt)
OOP classes: UpperCamelCase with Flode prefix (e.g., FlodeCatchment, FlodeForecast)
Variables: descriptive snake_case nouns (e.g., catchment_area_km2, peak_flow_cms)
Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., DEFAULT_THRESHOLD_M3S)
File names: descriptive, date-prefixed for scripts (e.g., 2026-02_flow_ensemble_aggregation.R)



6.2.2 2.2.2 Code Structure

Scripts must begin with a standardised header block (see Section 2.4)
Functions should follow the single-responsibility principle: one function, one task
Scripts should not exceed 300 lines; longer scripts should be refactored into functions or sub-scripts
Avoid hard-coded file paths; use relative paths or a centralised configuration file
Use the here package for portable path management



6.2.3 2.2.3 Package Dependencies and the fastverse
The team’s default package ecosystem is the fastverse – a suite of high-performance R packages optimised for speed and memory efficiency. The fastverse is preferred over the tidyverse for all data manipulation and numerical tasks in production tools.







Reason
Detail




Speed
data.table grouped operations and joins are typically an order of magnitude faster than dplyr equivalents on large datasets.


Memory efficiency
data.table modifies objects in place by reference, avoiding copy-on-modify behaviour and reducing peak memory usage.


File I/O performance
data.table::fread() is the fastest general-purpose text file reader available in R.


Production stability
data.table has an exceptionally strong backwards-compatibility record. The tidyverse has introduced breaking changes across major versions.


Lean dependency footprint
The fastverse is leaner in terms of package dependencies than the tidyverse, simplifying renv lockfile management etc..



The tidyverse must not be used in Tier 1 operational tools or in Flode package functions. It may be used freely in Tier 3 exploratory work.







Task
Preferred Package(s)




Tabular data manipulation
data.table (primary); collapse as supplementary high-performance toolkit


Time series operations
kit, roll (from fastverse); avoid zoo/xts unless interfacing with external systems


Numerical / statistical computation
collapse::fnth(), collapse::fmean() etc.; avoid apply-family loops over large data


File I/O (tabular text)
data.table::fread() / fwrite() – never read.csv() or readr in production


File I/O (Parquet)
arrow::read_parquet() / write_parquet()


File I/O (spatial / netCDF)
terra, ncdf4 – approved for spatial and gridded data


Visualisation
ggplot2 acceptable for Tier 2–3; flode.viz functions preferred for standardised outputs (longer term)


Configuration / paths
here, config


Package development
devtools, roxygen2, usethis, testthat









Guidance for Newer R Users – data.table data.table syntax can look unfamiliar at first. The key concept is DT[i, j, by]: filter rows with i, select or compute columns with j, and group with by. The data.table wiki (rdatatable.gitlab.io/data.table/) has excellent worked examples. Ask the R Lead for a walkthrough session if you are new to it.







6.2.4 2.2.4 File Formats and Export Standards







Format
Recommended Use




Parquet (.parquet)
Preferred format for all large tabular outputs in production tools. Use arrow::write_parquet() and arrow::read_parquet().


CSV (.csv)
Acceptable for small exchange files (under ~10,000 rows). Use data.table::fwrite() exclusively.


netCDF (.nc)
Required for gridded spatial outputs. Use ncdf4 or terra.


RDS (.rds)
Acceptable for R-specific intermediate objects. Use saveRDS() / readRDS(). Do not use .RData files.


Feather (.feather)
Acceptable alternative to Parquet for high-speed intermediate files within a single pipeline.


Excel (.xlsx)
Restricted to final-output reports and stakeholder deliverables only. Use openxlsx2 if required.



For full technical detail on each format, including partitioning conventions, type requirements, spatial format comparisons, and the rationale for CSV and Excel restrictions, see Appendix E. Format compliance for Tier 1 and Tier 2 tools is checked automatically by the fw-governance MCP server check_file_formats tool.

6.3 2.3 Object-Oriented Programming in Flode
Where tools require stateful objects or extensible APIs, OOP is preferred. Flode adopts a clear hierarchy for which system to use.








System
When to Use
Avoid When




S7 (preferred for Flode)
Defining new classes in Flode modules; formal, validated class contracts; any new class exported from a Flode package
Rapid prototyping in Tier 3 scripts; simple one-off data containers


R6

S4
Interoperability with existing S4 packages (e.g., terra, sp) only
All new development – S7 supersedes S4

7.1 3.1 R Review Checklist
All reviewers must work through this checklist. The completed checklist must be attached to the pull request before merging.

7.1.1 A. Correctness

Does the code do what it claims to do in its documentation?
Have edge cases (empty inputs, NA values, out-of-range data) been handled?
Are any assumptions about input data explicitly stated?



7.1.2 B. Code Quality

Does the code follow team naming conventions and internal style standards?
Is the header block complete and accurate?
Are functions appropriately scoped and documented with roxygen2?
Is the code free of hard-coded file paths (use here)?
Is the correct OOP system used? Are S7 properties typed and validators present for Tier 1/2 classes? Do R6 classes have a print method?



7.1.3 C. Testing

Have testthat tests been written or updated (Tier 1 mandatory, Tier 2 recommended)?
Do existing tests pass?
Has the code been run against a representative input dataset?



7.1.4 D. Dependencies and Reproducibility

Are all packages declared and version-noted where necessary?
Is the renv.lock file updated and committed?
Can the tool be run from a fresh R session without undeclared dependencies?

7.5 4.2 Reproducibility with renv
All team R repositories must use renv to manage package dependencies. This ensures that code run today produces the same results when run by a colleague in the future.

Continuous Improvement: The framework is a living document, reviewed annually.

title: 4  Python Tool Governance
text:
7.1 2.1 Python Use Cases
Python tools in the team fall into two primary categories. Understanding which category a tool belongs to helps determine its appropriate dependencies, structure, and tier.

7.1.1 2.1.1 Flood Modeller API Integration
The Flood Modeller API is a Python interface for driving Flood Modeller Pro model runs programmatically. Tools in this category typically: read data prepared by Flode (from Parquet or other outputs), construct and submit model runs via the API, retrieve and post-process results, and pass outputs back to Flode-compatible formats for further analysis.






Flode and Python Flode (the team’s R package) does not have a Python equivalent. Python tools consume Flode outputs rather than replicating its functions. The standard interface is Parquet files written by Flode and read in Python using pyarrow or polars. Do not replicate Flode data processing in Python – if data preparation logic needs to change, change it in Flode.







7.1.2 2.1.2 Machine Learning Tools
ML tools cover the full model development lifecycle: data preparation, feature engineering, model training, validation, and inference. Key standards for ML tools are:

Training and inference must be separated into distinct scripts or modules
All trained model artefacts must be versioned and stored with a JSON metadata file describing training data, hyperparameters, and evaluation scores unless captured in MLFlow processes.
Evaluation scripts must be reproducible: fixed random seeds (if required), documented train/test splits, and version-pinned dependencies
Inference pipelines used operationally are Tier 1 regardless of how the model was trained

title: 4  Python Tool Governance
text:
7.2 2.2 Coding Style and Conventions
All team Python code follows PEP 8, with the additions below.

7.2.1 2.2.1 Naming Conventions

Functions and methods: snake_case verbs (e.g., run_model_scenario(), load_parquet_data())
Variables: descriptive snake_case nouns (e.g., catchment_area_km2, peak_flow_cms)
Classes: PascalCase (e.g., FloodModelRunner, EnsembleForecast)
Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., DEFAULT_THRESHOLD_M3S, API_TIMEOUT_S)
Modules and packages: lowercase, short, no hyphens (e.g., flood_api, ml_pipeline)
File names: descriptive, date-prefixed for scripts (e.g., 2026-02_scenario_batch_run.py)



7.2.2 2.2.2 Type Hints
All function signatures in shared modules and Tier 1–2 scripts must include type hints. Type correctness is checked with mypy as part of CI (see Section 3.2).


7.2.3 2.2.3 Package Dependencies and the polars Ecosystem
The team’s default data manipulation library is polars, not pandas. This mirrors the R framework’s preference for the fastverse: the team processes large volumes of tabular data, and performance and memory efficiency matter.







Reason
Detail




Speed
polars uses a lazy evaluation engine built on Apache Arrow and Rust. For large DataFrames, polars is consistently faster than pandas, often by an order of magnitude for grouped and aggregated operations.


Memory efficiency
polars does not copy data unnecessarily. pandas’ copy-on-modify behaviour leads to high peak memory usage. polars stores all data as typed Arrow arrays.


Consistency with Flode I/O
Flode writes Parquet via the arrow package. polars reads Parquet natively via its own Arrow integration. Data types and column schemas are preserved exactly.


Explicit lazy evaluation
polars’ lazy API allows downstream tools to read only the columns and rows they need from large Flode outputs, without loading the full dataset into memory.


Type safety
polars enforces strict typing across columns. pandas allows mixed-type columns and silent type coercions that can cause hard-to-debug errors in operational pipelines.



pandas must not be used in Tier 1 operational tools or in shared modules. It may be used freely in Tier 3 exploratory work and Jupyter notebooks.






Guidance for Newer Python Users – polars If you are used to pandas, polars syntax will feel slightly different. The key shift is that polars expressions are evaluated lazily and column operations are written as expressions: df.select(pl.col(‘flow_cms’).mean().alias(‘mean_flow’)). The polars user guide at docs.pola.rs is the recommended starting point. Ask the Delegated Steward for a walkthrough if you are new to it.

Format
Use in Python Tools

Primary format for reading Flode outputs and writing large tabular results. Use polars or pyarrow.

Small exchange files only. Use polars: df.write_csv(). Never use pandas read_csv / to_csv in production tools.

Gridded spatial data. Use xarray / rioxarray, consistent with R’s use of terra/ncdf4.

Not recommended for shared or archived model artefacts. Use joblib for scikit-learn models or the framework’s native format for deep learning.

Preferred format for archiving trained ML models intended for long-term operational use.

All trained ML model artefacts saved to disk must be accompanied by a JSON metadata file containing: training date, Python and package versions, training dataset identifier, hyperparameters, and key evaluation metrics.
