title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
6 1. Purpose
The Flood Forecast Modelling (FFM) and Warning teams import hydrometric data - flow, stage, and rainfall records - from a range of internal systems (Hydrology Data Explorer and WISKI) as well as external suppliers including SEPA, NRW, Met Office, and other partner organisations. These data are the foundation of everything the team does: they drive model calibration, feed operational forecasts, validate modelling outputs, and inform flood risk decisions.
Without a clear framework, the risks are real: data used at different stages of processing gets confused with raw data, quality problems go unnoticed until they affect a model output, provenance is lost making it impossible to audit where a number came from, and the same cleaning work gets done repeatedly by different people with different results.
This framework addresses those risks by defining how imported hydrometric data moves through three quality tiers: Bronze, Silver, and Gold - from raw ingestion to analysis-ready products. It sets out who owns and is responsible for data at each tier, how quality is assessed and recorded, how provenance is tracked, how data is stored, and how data quality is improved over time.
The parent framework (Chapter 2) defines two distinct classification systems that apply to all team assets. The operational tier system (Tier 1, 2, 3) answers the question: how critical is this asset to the live forecasting service? The medallion architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold) answers a different question: how far has this data progressed through the quality assurance process?
For code tools and models these two dimensions often align closely. For hydrometric data they are genuinely independent, and that independence matters. A Silver dataset for the River Wye may be used in a Tier 2 post-event analysis today and promoted to supply a Tier 1 operational model tomorrow, without changing anything about the data itself. A Gold approved benchmark series for a small catchment may only ever be used in Tier 3 research. The operational tier describes the use; the medallion tier describes the data’s quality state. Conflating them would mean re-approving data every time its purpose changes, which is neither practical nor meaningful.
The medallion architecture was developed in data engineering for exactly the problem the team faces: data arriving from multiple external sources, at different quality levels, needing to flow through defined processing stages before being fit for production use. It maps directly onto the hydrometric data lifecycle. Supplier data arrives raw and unmodified (Bronze). The team applies quality control, flags anomalies, applies rating curves, and documents decisions (Silver). Derived products, aggregated statistics, calibration benchmarks, and ML training sets are assembled from Silver and formally approved (Gold). Each stage represents a distinct level of trust and a distinct degree of accountability. Bronze data is not worse than Silver data; it is simply at a different stage. Storing them as separate, preserved states makes that explicit.
Taken together, the two frameworks give the team three things it cannot get from informal arrangements. Reproducibility: any formal output can be traced back through Gold to Silver to Bronze to the exact file received from the supplier, with every quality decision recorded along the way. Efficiency: QC work invested at Silver is done once and available to everyone, rather than each analyst reworking the same dataset for their own purpose and potentially reaching different conclusions. Confidence: a Gold product carries a specific meaning. It has passed through defined stages, had decisions documented, and been formally approved for an identified purpose. When a Gold dataset feeds a Tier 1 model run, the team knows precisely what it is, who reviewed it, and what it has been approved for. That chain of accountability is the point.
Imported hydrometric data passes through three tiers of increasing quality and fitness for purpose. The tiers are named Bronze, Silver, and Gold - a medallion structure adapted from data engineering practice to suit hydrological data management.
The key principle is that each tier is a distinct, preserved state. Data is never overwritten in place. Moving data to the next tier creates a new dataset; the previous tier is always retained. This means the team can always trace exactly what was received, what quality decisions were made, and what version of a dataset fed a particular model run.
All Bronze, Silver, and Gold datasets are stored as Parquet files. Parquet is the mandatory storage format for hydrometric time series data within the medallion architecture. It is used across the R tooling (via the arrow package) and the Python tooling (via polars or pyarrow), and it is the native format for the Databricks DASH environment.
Parquet stores data in a typed, columnar format that is efficient to read, write, and query even for very long time series. Unlike CSV, it preserves data types exactly (timestamps, integers, floats) and is compressed automatically, which matters for long multi-year records at 15-minute resolution.
For the rationale behind the Parquet requirement, partitioning guidance, format comparisons (including Delta tables, NetCDF, GeoParquet, and the CSV and Excel restrictions), see Appendix E. Parquet schema compliance for Bronze, Silver, and Gold datasets is checked automatically by the fw-governance MCP server validate_parquet_schema and validate_bronze_ingestion tools.
The medallion structure is not just a filing system; it is a mechanism for identifying and acting on data quality problems over time. Quality issues discovered at Silver or Gold should feed back into improved processes and, where possible, improved data from suppliers.
Every formal output the team produces must be traceable back to the data that fed it. The Bronze to Silver to Gold chain provides that traceability, but only if it is used consistently.
The Hydrometric Data Register is the single consolidated record for all Bronze, Silver, and Gold datasets. It is maintained by the reach.io R package as a CSV file held in the team’s designated data store, version-controlled alongside the data. Register entries are written and updated programmatically via reach.io’s write_provenance_record() function; direct manual editing of the CSV is not permitted outside of Steward-approved corrections. In Databricks deployments, the same fields are held as a Delta table in the fw_hydrometric catalog. The Steward is responsible for keeping it current.
A separate Gauge Registry (Parquet format) is also maintained by reach.io via build_gauge_registry(). It is the routing configuration for the ingestion pipeline and records, for each gauge: source system assignment, active status, backfill completion flag, and notes. Changes to the Gauge Registry require Steward approval and are committed with a brief note describing the reason.
Rather than separate provenance, QC, and derivation records for each tier, the register uses a single table where each row is one dataset. The tier column identifies whether a row is Bronze, Silver, or Gold. Fields that only apply to certain tiers are left blank for others. This keeps everything queryable in one place and avoids the proliferation of separate files.
The roles below follow the Owner, Steward, and Custodian model defined in the Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2023) and applied in the Data & Digital Asset Governance Framework v1.4. The specific responsibilities at each tier are summarised here. The Data Owner for hydrometric data assets fulfils the Information Asset Owner (IAO) function for those assets; see Section 2.3.6 in the parent framework for the full role mapping.
This framework is reviewed annually by the Steward and approved by the Owner. The review considers:
Exceptions to this framework - for example, using Bronze data directly in an urgent operational run - must be documented in the run record and reported to the Delegated Steward. Repeated exceptions in the same area should trigger a review of whether the Silver pipeline needs to be accelerated for that data source.
All dataset IDs use underscores, no spaces, no dots except as the file extension.
Supplier codes: EA = Environment Agency, NRFA = National River Flow Archive, MO = Met Office, CEH = Centre for Ecology & Hydrology. [Other] = agree with Steward before first use.
Data type codes: Q = flow, H = stage/water level, P = rainfall, SM = soil moisture, SWE = snow water equivalent.
The following shows the recommended folder structure for hydrometric data storage, covering both the team file store and the Databricks DASH environment.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
6.1 2. Scope
This framework covers all hydrometric data imported and used by the Flood Forecast Modelling Team, including:

River flow and water level records from gauging stations (telemetry and archived)
Rating metadata
Rainfall records from rain gauges and gridded weather radar products
Catchment-averaged rainfall products
Snow measurements
MOSES PE and similar products
Soil moisture data e.g. Copernicus
Historical event datasets used for model calibration and validation







Out of Scope: Model outputs, internally generated datasets (e.g., ensemble forecasts), and data produced by the team’s own tools are governed by the Data & Digital Asset Governance Framework and are not covered here. Internally generated data does not pass through the Bronze to Silver to Gold pipelines.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
8.1 4.1 Ingestion Requirements
When a new dataset is received, the Custodian must complete all of the following before the data is stored:

Assign a unique dataset ID using the standard format: [SupplierCode][SiteID][DataType]_[YYYYMMDD] (e.g., EA_39001_Q_20260115)
Record the full provenance record (see Section 4.2) in the Hydrometric Data Register via reach.io’s write_provenance_record() function
Store the data in the Bronze layer of the team’s data store using reach.io’s directory structure (created by setup_hydro_store()); do not modify the file
Apply the Bronze schema using apply_bronze_schema() to enforce the six mandatory columns (timestamp, value, supplier_flag, dataset_id, site_id, data_type) and correct data types
Check the file opens and is readable; record any format issues in the provenance record
Notify the Steward that a new Bronze dataset has been ingested

For API-sourced gauges registered in the Gauge Registry, reach.io’s run_backfill() and route_gauge() functions automate the fetch, schema application, and provenance recording steps. The Custodian is still responsible for reviewing the resulting register entry and confirming completeness.
Bronze data must never be modified after ingestion. If a supplier sends a corrected version of a dataset, the corrected version is ingested as a new Bronze dataset with its own dataset ID and provenance record, referencing the original.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
8.2 4.2 Provenance Record
Every Bronze dataset must have a complete provenance record in the Hydrometric Data Register (Section 10). This is the single most important thing recorded at Bronze - without it, no downstream use of the data can be properly audited. See Section 10.1 for the full field list.
The key fields recorded at ingestion are: dataset ID, supplier, site identifier, data type, time period, temporal resolution, units, datum or rating reference, file format as received, date received, received by, method of receipt, any supplier quality flags and their meaning, known limitations stated by the supplier, file path, and any notes on unusual aspects of the delivery.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
8.3 4.3 Ownership at Bronze
The Custodian who ingests the data holds Bronze custodianship. They are responsible for completing the provenance record and storing the data correctly. The Steward is responsible for checking that provenance records are complete and that Bronze data is not being modified.
Bronze data is owned by the team collectively - it represents an external input and no individual team member has the right to modify or delete it. Deletion of Bronze data requires Owner approval and must be documented.
4.4 What Bronze Data Is Not For
Bronze data is an archive, not a working dataset. It should not be:

Used directly as input to a model or analysis without Silver processing
Shared externally (the supplier’s data licence applies - check before sharing)
Modified to fix errors, even obvious ones
Used to draw conclusions about data quality without a Silver QC record

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.1 5.1 The QC Process
Quality control must be completed by a Custodian and reviewed by the Steward before data is promoted from Bronze to Silver. The QC process covers four stages:

9.1.1 Stage 1: Automated Checks
Run automated checks to identify obvious problems. These checks do not change any values - they produce a flag dataset stored alongside the data. Automated checks include:

Range checks: values outside physically plausible bounds for the variable and site (e.g., negative flow, unrealistic stage)
Rate-of-change checks: implausible step changes between consecutive time-steps
Flatline detection: sequences of identical repeated values (sensor malfunction indicator)
Gap detection: missing values, irregular time-steps, or gaps relative to the stated period
Duplicate detection: repeated timestamps
Consistency with supplier flags: values flagged as poor quality by the supplier



9.1.2 Stage 2: Visual and Expert Review
A Custodian with appropriate domain knowledge reviews the flagged data. For flow and level data this includes checking against nearby gauges, upstream/downstream consistency, and known events. The review produces:

A revised flag dataset - each value receives a quality flag (see Section 5.2)
A review note for any value that is flagged as suspect or rejected
A rating curve assessment for flow data (see Section 5.3)



9.1.3 Stage 3: Gap and Error Handling
For each gap or rejected value, the Custodian must make a documented decision:







Decision
When to apply




Retain as flagged
The value is suspect but not clearly wrong; retain with a ‘suspect’ flag so downstream users can decide whether to use it


Reject and leave as gap
The value is clearly wrong (e.g., sensor malfunction) and no suitable substitute is available; record the gap extent and reason


Gap-fill with documented method
A gap can be filled using a defensible method (e.g., correlation with nearby gauge, simple interpolation for short gaps); the fill method, source data, and uncertainty estimate must all be recorded


Reject the entire dataset
If data quality is too poor to be useful even with flagging, the dataset is rejected at Silver; document the reasons and retain Bronze



Gap-filling is only permitted where the method is documented and the filled values are clearly distinguishable from observed values. Over-enthusiastic gap-filling is a greater risk than gaps. When in doubt, flag and retain rather than fill.


9.1.4 Stage 4: Steward Review and Promotion
Before data is promoted to Silver, the Steward or Delegated Steward must review:

That the QC process has been followed and documented
That flagging decisions are consistent with team standards
That any gap-filling is justified and documented
That the Silver dataset ID and QC record are complete

The Steward records their approval in the Hydrometric Data Register. Only after Steward approval is the dataset status set to Silver.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.2 5.2 Quality Flags
Every value in a Silver dataset carries a quality flag. The team uses the following flag scheme, which is compatible with the Environment Agency’s national flag convention:









Flag
Label
Meaning
Use in modelling




1
Good
Passed all automated checks; expert review confirms no concerns
Use without restriction


2
Estimated
Observed value is missing or rejected; value has been estimated using a documented method
Use with caution; document in run records


3
Suspect
Value appears anomalous but cannot be confirmed as wrong; retained for user judgement
Exclude by default; include only if explicitly justified


4
Rejected
Value is confirmed as erroneous; treated as missing
Do not use


5
No data
Timestep is genuinely missing with no basis for estimation
Do not use


6
Below detection
Value is below the instrument’s detection limit; record the limit
Use as threshold information only



Flags must be stored as a separate column or parallel file - never overwrite the value itself. A flag of 2 (Estimated) must always be accompanied by an estimation method field.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.3 5.3 Rating Curves and Flow Derivation
For stage (water level) data where the team derives flow using a rating curve, the Silver record must include:

The rating curve version used (name, version number, valid stage range, source/authority)
The date the rating curve was applied
Any values where stage falls outside the rated range, flagged separately as ‘extrapolated’
A note of any known shift events (e.g., channel changes, weed growth) that may affect the rating

Where the team uses supplier-derived flow directly (e.g., EA gauged flow), the supplier’s rating version must be recorded in the provenance record rather than applied by the team.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.4 5.4 Silver Dataset Naming and Storage
Each Silver dataset gets its own dataset ID, linking it explicitly to its Bronze source:
Format: [BronzeDatasetID]_SILVER_v[N] Example: EA_39001_Q_20260115_SILVER_v1
When a Silver dataset is revised (e.g., following updated rating curve or additional QC), a new version is created. Previous Silver versions are retained. The QC record must note what changed and why.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.5 5.5 Silver QC Record
Each Silver dataset must have a complete QC record in the Hydrometric Data Register (Section 10). See Section 10.1 for the full field list.
The key fields recorded at Silver promotion are: Silver dataset ID, Bronze source ID, Custodian who carried out QC, Steward who reviewed and approved, QC date, automated checks run and tool used, flag count summary by type, gap-filling method and extent if applied, rating curve version and valid range if applied, any remaining known issues, comparison datasets used during expert review, and file path.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
9.6 5.6 Ownership at Silver
The Steward or Delegated Steward holds Silver ownership. They are accountable for the quality of Silver datasets and for ensuring QC records are complete and honest - including about limitations. The Custodian who carried out the QC is named in the record and is responsible for the decisions made during QC.
Silver data is the primary working dataset. Modellers and analysts should use Silver data and record which Silver dataset ID (and version) fed their work. If a modeller identifies a quality issue in Silver data, they must raise it with the Steward rather than correcting it locally.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
10.1 6.1 What Qualifies as Gold
A Gold dataset is a deliberate, named product created for a specific purpose. Examples include:

Catchment-averaged rainfall series constructed from multiple rain gauge Silver records
Multi-site composite records where gaps at one site are filled from a correlated site
ML training set: a named, approved collection of 15-minute Silver time series data with static catchment attributes attached, covering a defined period and gauge selection, with flag exclusion rules documented and Steward sign-off that Silver quality is sufficient for model training
Event hydrographs used in calibrations and post event analytics.
Aggregated data such as annual maximum flow series for a gauge used in flood frequency analysis
Daily mean flow record for a catchment, approved as the reference series for model calibration
Design event hydrograph derived from observed events in Silver data
Benchmark period dataset (agreed period used for inter-annual comparison)

Gold is not simply ‘better Silver’. It is a specific product with a defined purpose, a named user, and formal approval. Creating a Gold dataset is a decision, not an automatic step.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
10.2 6.2 Creating a Gold Dataset
A Gold dataset must be proposed, documented, and approved before it is used:

Custodian or modeller proposes the Gold product, specifying: its purpose, which Silver datasets it draws from, the derivation method, and the intended use
Steward reviews the proposal and the underlying Silver data quality, particularly flag counts and known issues
Derivation is carried out and documented in a Gold derivation record (see Section 6.3)
Owner reviews and formally approves the Gold dataset before it enters operational use
Gold dataset is registered in the Hydrometric Data Register with status ‘Approved’

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
10.3 6.3 Gold Derivation Record
Each Gold dataset must have a complete derivation record in the Hydrometric Data Register (Section 10). See Section 10.1 for the full field list.
The key fields recorded when a Gold dataset is created are: Gold dataset ID, purpose and who approved it, Silver source dataset IDs and versions, derivation method (aggregation, merging, event extraction, or native resolution for ML training sets), Silver quality gate summary (flag counts, gap extent, known issues), any exclusions and the reason, Custodian or analyst who produced it, Owner approval name and date, intended use and any restrictions on use, expiry or review date, and file path.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
10.4 6.4 Versioning and Supersession
When new Silver data becomes available, or when a quality issue is identified, a Gold dataset may need to be updated. A new version is created; the previous version is retained and its status changed to ‘Superseded’. Any model or analysis that used the superseded version must be flagged for review.
The Steward or Delegated Steward must be notified whenever a Gold dataset is superseded and must confirm whether dependent work needs to be revisited.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
10.5 6.5 Ownership at Gold
Gold datasets are owned by the Owner and stewarded by the Steward. No one else can approve a new Gold dataset or change its status. This is the highest accountability level because Gold data directly informs business decisions, model calibration choices, and potentially regulatory outputs or KPIs.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
section: 10.6 6.6 ML Training Sets as Gold Products
text:
10.6 6.6 ML Training Sets as Gold Products
Unlike most Gold products, an ML training set does not aggregate or reduce the underlying Silver data. It stays at the native 15-minute resolution. What makes it a Gold product is that it represents a set of deliberate, documented decisions about which data to use and how, combined with Steward confirmation that the Silver quality is sufficient for model training.
A Silver dataset is ready to become a Gold ML training set when all of the following conditions are met:

The time series data has been promoted to Silver and has a complete QC record including flag counts, gap assessment, and rating curve version where applicable
Static catchment attributes have been calculated and attached, covering at minimum: catchment area, BFI, mean elevation, dominant soil type, and land cover class
The training period has been defined and the flag exclusion rule has been documented (e.g., which flag types cause a timestep to be dropped from training)
Gap-filling decisions for the training period have been recorded, including method
and extent
The Steward has reviewed the Silver quality and confirmed it is sufficient for the intended model type and promotion tier

The Gold derivation record for an ML training set should describe the gauge selection rationale, the training period, and the static attribute sources alongside the standard fields. The derivation method field should state that no temporal aggregation has been applied and that the dataset is at native 15-minute resolution.






This training set Gold product type is distinct from other Gold types. It should not be used for flood frequency analysis or hydraulic model calibration, and those Gold products should not be used as ML training sets without a new Gold derivation record confirming suitability.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
section: 11.1 7.1 Why Parquet for Hydrometric Time Series
text:
11.1 7.1 Why Parquet for Hydrometric Time Series







Reason
Detail




Type safety
Timestamps are stored as datetime64[ns, UTC] rather than strings. Floats are float64 throughout. Integers (flags, counts) are int32. This prevents silent type errors when data is read by different tools.


Columnar reads
Downstream tools can read only the columns they need (e.g., just timestamp and value) without loading the full file. This is important for long records across hundreds of gauges.


Compression
Parquet uses Snappy compression by default, reducing storage by 60-80% compared to equivalent CSV files with no loss of data.


Cross-tool compatibility
The same Parquet file can be read by R (arrow::read_parquet), Python (polars.read_parquet / pyarrow), and Databricks (spark.read.parquet) without conversion.


Partition support
Large datasets can be partitioned by supplier, site, or year, so queries only scan the relevant subset of files.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
11.2 7.2 Bronze Parquet Schema
Bronze Parquet is produced at ingestion. The Custodian converts the supplier’s raw file into the team’s standard Bronze schema. The original raw file is also retained unchanged. All dataset-level metadata (supplier, time period, units, licence, file format, etc.) is recorded in the register, not repeated in the Parquet.
Mandatory columns:








Column
Type
Description




timestamp
timestamp[ns, UTC]
Observation datetime in UTC. Convert supplier local times at ingestion and record the offset in the register.


value
float64
Observed value as received from supplier. Do not round or convert units. Preserve the supplier’s precision.


supplier_flag
string
Quality code or flag exactly as provided by the supplier. Null if the supplier provides no flags.


dataset_id
string
The Bronze dataset ID (e.g., EA_39001_Q_20260115). The join key to the register. Stored in every row so merged files remain traceable.


site_id
string
Supplier’s site identifier. Preserved exactly as received.


data_type
string
Data type code: Q, H, P, SM, or SWE.



Optional columns (include if provided by supplier):








Column
Type
Description




raw_value_str
string
The value as a raw string before parsing. Retain where the supplier uses special markers (e.g., “>” for above-range values).


uncertainty
float64
Measurement uncertainty if stated by supplier.


sensor_id
string
Instrument or sensor ID where the supplier provides this.









Do not add any columns beyond those listed above to Bronze Parquet. Bronze is a faithful representation of what was received. Any derived or computed fields belong in Silver.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
11.3 7.3 Silver Parquet Schema
Silver Parquet is derived from Bronze. It retains all Bronze columns and adds QC columns. Values and timestamps from Bronze are never altered - corrections and estimates are recorded in new columns, not by overwriting the Bronze value.
Added columns (in addition to all Bronze columns):








Column
Type
Description




qc_flag
int32
Team quality flag (1=Good, 2=Estimated, 3=Suspect, 4=Rejected, 5=No data, 6=Below detection). See Section 5.2. Every row must have a qc_flag at Silver.


qc_value
float64
The value to use for analysis. Equal to value for Good data. For Estimated rows, this is the gap-filled or estimated value. For Rejected or No data rows, this is null. Never overwrite value; always populate qc_value separately.


estimation_method
string
How qc_value was estimated for flag=2 rows (e.g., “linear_interpolation”, “correlation_gauge_39002”, “mean_seasonal”). Null for all other flags.


rating_curve_version
string
Version of the rating curve applied to derive flow from stage. Null for direct supplier flow or non-flow data types.


extrapolated
bool
True where stage falls outside the valid range of the rating curve. Null for non-flow data.


silver_dataset_id
string
The Silver dataset ID (e.g., EA_39001_Q_20260115_SILVER_v1). Stored in every row.


qc_version
int32
Version number of the Silver dataset (1, 2, 3…). Increments when QC is revised.









The value column is always the Bronze value. The qc_value column is what modellers and analysts should use. Keeping both means the QC decisions are always auditable.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
11.4 7.4 Gold Parquet Schema
Gold Parquet is derived from Silver. The schema depends on the Gold product type. Two standard structures are defined below.
Time Series Gold (calibration inputs, benchmark series)
For Gold products that are still time series (e.g., a daily mean flow series approved for model calibration), use the Silver schema with the following additional columns. Dataset-level approval details are held in the register, not repeated per row.








Column
Type
Description

string
The Gold dataset ID (e.g., 39001_Q_GOLD_FFA_v1). Join key to the register. Stored in every row.


gold_version
int32
Version number of the Gold dataset.


flag_exclusion_rule
string
The flag exclusion rule applied when deriving Gold from Silver (e.g., “exclude_flags_3_4_5”). Stored in every row so the rule is self-documenting even in extracted subsets.



The qc_value column from Silver is the source value for Gold time series. Rejected and No data rows (flags 4 and 5) are typically excluded; the flag_exclusion_rule column records exactly which flags were dropped.
Aggregated Gold (statistics, design events, frequency analysis inputs)
For Gold products that aggregate Silver time series into statistics or event summaries, use a purpose-specific schema. At minimum include:








Column
Type
Description

string
Gold dataset ID. Join key to the register.


site_id
string
Site or catchment identifier

date32
Start of the aggregation period


period_end
date32
End of the aggregation period


[statistic columns]
float64
e.g., annual_max_flow_m3s, peak_rainfall_mm, mean_daily_flow_m3s. Name columns with units as suffix.


data_completeness_pct
float64
Percentage of the period covered by Good or Estimated Silver data (flags 1 and 2).

string

11.4.1 ML Training Set Gold
For Gold ML training sets (Section 6.6), use the time series Gold schema with the following additional columns. Static catchment attributes are repeated on every row so a single Parquet file is self-contained for training without needing a join. Approval details are held in the register.








Column
Type
Description

string
Gold dataset ID for this ML training set (e.g., 39001_Q_GOLD_LSTM_v1). Join key to the register.


flag_exclusion_rule
string
Flag exclusion rule applied (e.g., exclude_flags_3_4_5). Stored in every row.


catchment_area_km2
float64
Catchment area in km².

float64
Base Flow Index (0 to 1). Source and version held in the register derivation record.


mean_elevation_m
float64
Mean catchment elevation in metres above ordnance datum.


dominant_soil_type
string
Dominant soil class from the HOST classification (e.g., HOST_1, HOST_29).

string
Dominant land cover class (e.g., improved_grassland, arable, woodland). Source dataset in register.

float64

float64
Gauge location northing in OSGB36 (metres).









Static attributes are repeated on every row so the file is self-contained for training. A pipeline loads one file and gets both the time series and catchment descriptors. The source dataset and version for each attribute must be recorded in the register derivation record, not in the Parquet itself.





For large datasets covering many sites or long time periods, Parquet files should be partitioned to avoid loading unnecessary data. The recommended partition scheme is:

In Databricks, use Delta Lake tables rather than raw Parquet files for Bronze and Silver stores. Delta Lake provides transaction safety, schema enforcement, and time-travel queries on top of the Parquet format. The column schemas above apply to Delta Lake tables identically.






The Parquet schemas defined in this section are the interface contract between the Hydrometric Data Framework and the AI/ML Test Environment. The ML training pipeline reads Gold Parquet using the column names and types defined in Sections 7.3 and 7.4. Any schema changes must be agreed between the Steward and the Delegated Steward before implementation.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
12.1 8.1 Flagging Systemic Issues
When a Custodian or Steward identifies a recurring quality problem - a gauge that consistently produces flatline values during high flows, a supplier format that loses trailing zeros, a rating curve that is clearly outdated - this should be escalated as a systemic issue rather than handled case by case. Systemic issues are recorded in the Data Quality Issue Log and assigned to the Delegated Steward to manage.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
12.2 8.2 Supplier Engagement
Where a Bronze dataset contains quality problems that originate with the supplier (instrument failures, incorrect datum, outdated rating), the Delegated Steward should:

Document the issue precisely in the Silver QC record
Raise the issue with the supplier in writing, referencing the specific time periods affected
Request a corrected dataset where one is available
Record the outcome of the engagement in the Data Quality Issue Log

The team should not routinely correct supplier errors at Silver without engaging the supplier first, unless the operational need is urgent and documented. Correcting supplier errors silently means the supplier never improves.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
12.3 8.3 Rating Curve Reviews
Rating curves age. Channel geometry changes after flood events, vegetation and weed growth affects stage-discharge relationships seasonally, and structural changes at gauging stations invalidate previous curves. The Delegated Steward is responsible for:

Maintaining a rating curve review schedule for all sites where the team applies its own rating
Flagging in the Silver record when a rating review is overdue
Requesting updated rating information from the gauge operators where the team relies on a supplier rating
Triggering a Silver version update whenever a new rating curve is applied

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
12.4 8.4 Data Quality Metrics and Reporting
The Steward produces a quarterly data quality summary covering:

Number of active Bronze datasets, Silver datasets (by flag profile), and Gold datasets
Datasets awaiting Silver promotion (backlog)
Open Data Quality Issue Log entries and their age
Supplier engagement outcomes in the quarter
Rating curves flagged as overdue for review

The summary is shared with the Owner and reported at the team’s quarterly governance review.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
13.1 9.1 Dataset Lineage
For any Gold dataset, it must be possible to answer:

Which Bronze datasets contributed? What were their provenance records?
Which Silver processing steps were applied, and by whom?
What flags are present in the Silver data feeding this Gold product?
Has the supplier’s original data been corrected? If so, how, why, and by whom?

The Hydrometric Data Register (Section 10) maintains this lineage by linking Gold IDs to Silver IDs to Bronze IDs.

When a model run uses hydrometric data, the run record must specify:

The Gold or Silver dataset ID(s) used, including version
The time period extracted
Any flags excluded from the analysis and the exclusion rule applied

Bronze datasets are never deleted (see Section 11.1)
Silver versions are retained even when superseded
Gold versions are retained even when superseded, with their status changed to ‘Superseded’
The Hydrometric Data Register is backed up as part of the team’s standard data backup process

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
14.2 10.2 Data Quality Issue Log
The Data Quality Issue Log is a separate CSV file held alongside the Hydrometric Data Register (or a second Delta table in Databricks deployments). It records known quality problems that require action beyond routine QC. Each entry includes:

Issue ID and date raised
Dataset(s) affected (Bronze and/or Silver IDs)
Description of the issue
Whether the issue originates with the supplier or with team processing
Action taken or planned, and by whom
Date resolved and how

The log is reviewed by the Steward monthly and included in the quarterly data quality summary.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
14.3 10.3 Register Maintenance
The register must be updated whenever:

A new Bronze dataset is ingested
A Silver dataset is promoted, revised, or rejected
A Gold dataset is created, superseded, or withdrawn
A data quality issue is raised, progressed, or resolved
A supplier delivers a corrected or updated dataset

The register is version-controlled. The Delegated Steward commits changes with a note describing what was updated. Previous versions are retained as part of the retrospective traceability requirement.

title: 5  Imported Hydrometric Data Framework
text:
15.1 11.1 Retention
Bronze data are retained indefinitely. It is the permanent record of what was received and cannot be recreated. It must never be deleted without Owner approval.
Silver data is retained for as long as the Bronze data it was derived from is retained. Superseded Silver versions are kept alongside the current version with their status clearly labelled.
Gold data is retained for as long as any model, output, or decision that used it may need to be audited. In practice this is indefinitely for any Gold dataset that contributed to a formal flood risk output.

text:
15.2 11.2 Access

Gold: All team members have read access. Creating or superseding a Gold dataset requires Owner approval
External sharing of any tier requires Owner approval and must respect the supplier’s data licence

Most hydrometric data supplied by external organisations carries restrictions on redistribution. The provenance record must note the licence or access terms under which data was received. The Steward is responsible for:

Checking licence terms before any external sharing of Bronze or Silver data
Ensuring that Gold datasets derived from restricted data carry the same restrictions
Flagging any licence ambiguity to the Owner before sharing

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
7 Purpose
This document sets out detailed governance standards for the flood models used and maintained by the Forecasting and Warning (F&W) team. It covers Flood Modeller Pro hydraulic models, PDM rainfall-runoff models, Black Box elements, and the boundary conditions that connect them. It is a companion to the Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework, which sets out the broader roles, tier system, and version control principles that apply to all team assets.
Two areas are given particular attention here. First, model condition: a structured way of assessing how fit for purpose a model is over time, accounting for factors beyond operational performance alone, including age, data currency, structural integrity, and known deficiencies. Second, model connections: how models are linked together in cascading systems, where the outputs of one model become the inputs to another, and what governance is required to keep those connections auditable and reliable.
This framework applies to all flood models used by the F&W team in operational forecasting, model development, or research activities, including:
The team operates four categories of flood model. Each has distinct governance needs reflecting its structure, how it is calibrated, and how it sits within the broader modelling system.
Every flood model used by the team must be entered in the Model Register at the point it is used in a formal output or shared with another team member. The register is version-controlled and held in the team repository. It is distinct from the Tool Register in the parent framework, which covers code tools; the Model Register covers the hydraulic and hydrological models themselves.
The Steward is responsible for keeping the Model Register current. It must be updated whenever a model changes tier, a new calibrated version is produced, a model’s condition rating changes, or a model is deprecated.
Model condition is an assessment of how fit for purpose a model is at a given point in time. It is distinct from model performance in a narrow operational sense. A model may still produce outputs within acceptable error bounds while being in poor condition: its input data may be out of date, its channel geometry may no longer reflect the physical system, its software version may be unsupported (assuming changes to FM module adaptor), or its calibration may have been carried out on data that does not represent current catchment behaviour.
Condition assessment is the mechanism by which the team identifies models that need investment before problems emerge in operational use, rather than after. It provides an auditable basis for prioritising model maintenance work and for informing decisions about when a model should be retired or rebuilt.
Flood forecasting systems are rarely a single model in isolation. In most catchments, the team operates cascading systems: PDM models produce catchment runoff that drives FMP hydraulic models; FMP models route flows downstream to become boundary conditions for further FMP models; tidal models set downstream boundaries for fluvial models; Black Boxes route flows between points or create behaviors that can’t be replicated in our hydraulic models.
Understanding these connections is essential for three reasons. First, an error or condition problem in an upstream model propagates downstream and affects every connected model’s outputs. Second, when a model is updated or recalibrated, the team needs to know which downstream models may be affected. Third, in an operational failure, knowing the connection structure allows the team to identify workarounds or manual overrides that maintain forecast coverage.
For every model run that produces a formal output such as performance testing, the Custodian must complete a run record. This is the mechanism by which any output can be traced back to the exact model version, input data, and boundary conditions used to produce it.
Calibration is the process of adjusting model parameters so that simulated outputs match observed data. Validation is testing those parameters against observed data not used in calibration. Both are required before a model can be promoted to Tier 1 and must be repeated whenever the model is significantly updated.
A model moves between tiers as its use becomes more established or as it is superseded. Promotion and deprecation follow the same principles as the tool tier system in the parent framework, with the additions below specific to flood models.
The Owner, Steward, and Custodian roles from the parent framework apply to all flood models. The following additions are specific to this document.
For coupled or cascading systems, custodianship is assigned separately for each model component. Where one person is the Custodian for both an upstream and a downstream model, the Steward must satisfy themselves that there is sufficient independent oversight of the connection between them. For Tier 1 cascades involving more than three connected models, the Steward should consider whether a dedicated system-level Custodian is warranted.
This document is reviewed annually alongside the parent framework and companion documents. The review is led by the Steward with Owner sign-off. The annual review considers:
The Delegated Steward conducts an annual audit of all Tier 1 models covering: condition rating currency, calibration record completeness, run record completeness for all formal outputs, Connection Register accuracy, and system diagram currency. Findings are reported to the Owner alongside the wider governance audit.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
9.1 2.1 Flood Modeller Pro (FMP) Hydraulic Models
FMP models simulate the movement of water through river channels and floodplains using 1D network schemes, 2D domain solvers, or linked 1D-2D configurations. They are the core hydraulic routing tools in the team’s operational system. For flood forecast modelling requirements we limit our use of these to1D simulations only, but also implement hydrological routing elements too such as Muskingum Cunge and it’s variable parameter variant.
FMP models require formal version control because they contain binary and configuration files that can change with each calibration update, boundary condition change, or software upgrade. A model that produces a formal output and a model that has been subsequently updated must both be retained, with the version used for each output clearly identified.
All FMP model files must follow the folder structure and naming conventions in the parent framework (Section 6). The Custodian is responsible for keeping model files in the agreed location and not on local machines or unmanaged drives.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
9.2 2.2 PDM Rainfall-Runoff Models
PDM models transform rainfall and potential evapotranspiration inputs into catchment runoff, which is then used as an inflow boundary to FMP hydraulic models or fed directly into operational forecasting systems. PDM configurations include a parameter set, a calibration record, and specification of the input data sources used.
Parameter sets are particularly sensitive assets. A parameter set produced by one analyst using one period of observed data may produce materially different outputs from a parameter set calibrated by a different analyst on a different period, even for the same catchment. This makes version control and calibration documentation critical.
Every PDM parameter set must be stored in the agreed repository rather than on individual machines. It must be named following the standard convention set out in the parent framework and accompanied by a calibration record covering the period, data sources, performance metrics, and any known limitations.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
9.3 2.3 Black Box Methods
Black Boxes are data-driven models that relate inputs directly to outputs without representing the physical processes in between. In the team’s operational context this includes** ****SEE BLACK BOX DOCUMENT ALAN SENT ME** .
Black Box models carry a specific governance risk: because their internal workings are not as easily physically interpretable, it can be difficult to identify when a model has become unreliable. The model condition framework in Section 4 is particularly important for Black Box models, as performance degradation may not be apparent until a significant event occurs.
All Black Boxesused in operational forecasting are Tier 1 assets. They must have a named Custodian, a documented training dataset, and a formal condition assessment on the schedule defined in Section 4.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
9.4 2.4 Boundary Conditions
Boundary conditions are the forcing inputs that drive model runs: upstream flow inflows, tidal water levels at downstream boundaries, lateral inflows from ungauged catchments, reservoir release rules, and operational interventions such as gate settings. They are distinct assets from the models themselves and require their own version control and documentation.
A boundary condition dataset is not simply a data file. It represents a set of decisions about what inputs are appropriate for a given model and scenario. Those decisions must be documented so that a model run can be reproduced and audited.








Boundary type
Source
Governance requirement




Upstream inflow
PDM output, gauged flow (Gold tier), or routed flow from upstream FMP model
Dataset ID and version recorded in run record; PDM parameter set version noted if PDM-derived


Tidal boundary

Supplier and product version noted; Gold-tier observed data where used for calibration


Lateral inflow

Method documented; any simplifying assumptions explicitly stated in run record


Structure and reservoir operating rules

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
11.1 4.1 Condition Factors
Model condition is assessed across five factors. Each factor is scored on a three-point scale: Good (2), Adequate (1), or Poor (0). The overall condition rating is the sum of the five scores, giving a range from 0 (critically poor) to 10 (fully current).









Factor
Good (2)
Adequate (1)
Poor (0)




Data currency
All input data sources current; rating curves reviewed within 3 years; boundary conditions reflect current system
One or more input data sources older than 3 years or flagged for review; rating curve review overdue
Input data materially out of date; rating curves known to be invalid; boundary conditions do not reflect current system


Structural integrity
Channel geometry surveyed within 5 years or no significant physical changes known; mesh and network validated against current system
Survey more than 5 years old but no significant physical changes identified; minor known discrepancies
Survey known to be materially out of date; significant physical changes (flood defence works, channel modifications) not incorporated


Calibration currency
Calibrated against events including at least one event within the last 5 years; performance metrics meet agreed thresholds
Last calibration event more than 5 years ago but no evidence of performance degradation; metrics within acceptable range
Calibration based solely on old events; performance against recent events below agreed thresholds; known deficiencies not addressed


Software and dependency currency
Running on a current supported software version; all dependencies maintained and tested
One version behind current release; dependencies functional but flagged for upgrade
Running on an unsupported or deprecated software version; known compatibility issues with current infrastructure


Documentation completeness
Full calibration record, run records, and model notes up to date; handover note current; all known issues logged
Calibration record present but not fully updated after recent changes; run records incomplete for some outputs
Calibration record missing or materially out of date; run records absent; no handover note

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
11.2 4.2 Condition Ratings








Score
Rating
Required action




9-10
Good
Routine monitoring. Review on standard cycle (see Section 4.3).


7-8
Satisfactory
No immediate action required. Identify improvement actions in the next maintenance cycle. Flag any Poor-scoring individual factors for attention.


5-6
Requires attention
A condition improvement plan must be agreed with the Steward within three months. The model may continue in operational use while the plan is active, with the Steward’s agreement. Known deficiencies must be noted in all run records.


3-4
Poor
Owner must be notified. A formal review is required within one month to decide whether the model continues in operational use, is suspended pending improvement, or is retired. Continued use requires Owner sign-off with documented rationale.

Critical
Model is suspended from operational use immediately pending Owner review. Emergency improvement or replacement is required. Route D (emergency) from the parent framework applies if urgent operational cover is needed.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
11.3 4.3 Review Schedule
Condition assessments are carried out on a rolling schedule. The schedule is set by the Steward and recorded in the Model Register.








Tier
Standard review cycle
Triggered review




Tier 1 - Operational
Annual
After any significant flood event where model performance can be assessed; after any physical change to the modelled system; after a software upgrade; on handover of custodianship. Automated methods can be introduced.


Tier 2 - Analytical
Every two years
After significant physical changes; after a major data update; on handover of custodianship


Tier 3 - Experimental

A triggered review does not reset the standard cycle clock. A model that receives a triggered review in month six of a twelve-month cycle is still due its standard review at month twelve unless the Steward decides otherwise.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
11.4 4.4 Condition and Model Connections
Where a model in poor condition provides inputs to downstream models, the condition risk propagates. If a PDM with a Poor calibration currency rating drives the upstream boundary of an FMP model, the FMP model’s outputs carry the same uncertainty regardless of the FMP model’s own condition score. The model connections register (Section 5) must be consulted during every condition assessment to identify whether a model’s condition affects connected models, and this must be recorded in the condition assessment note.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
12.1 5.1 Connection Types








Connection type
Description
Example




Upstream inflow
Output from one model (PDM runoff or upstream FMP routed flow) becomes the upstream boundary condition for a downstream model
PDM catchment runoff feeds FMP river reach as a lateral inflow


Downstream boundary
Output or agreed condition from one model sets the downstream boundary for another
Tidal model water levels set the downstream boundary for an FMP estuarial reach


Intermediate routing
A Black Box or simplified routing model transfers flows between two FMP reaches where a full model is not available
Transfer function routes gauged flow from one site to the upstream boundary of an FMP model


Ensemble feed
Multiple model instances or ensemble members provide probabilistic inputs to a downstream system
NWP ensemble rainfall feeds multiple PDM runs, whose spread of outputs drives an ensemble of FMP runs


*Manual override point** (is this done anywhere?)*
A point in the cascade where an operator can substitute a model output with an observed or manually estimated value
Gauged flow substituted for PDM output when real-time gauge data is available and reliable

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
12.2 5.2 Connection Register
Every operational connection between models must be recorded in the Connection Register. This is a single version-controlled file held alongside the Model Register. The Steward is responsible for keeping it current. It must be updated whenever a model is added, modified, or retired, and whenever a connection changes.







Field
Description




Connection ID
Unique identifier: [UpstreamModelID]TO[DownstreamModelID] (e.g., SEVERN_PDM_v2.1_TO_SEVERN_FMP_v3.2)


Upstream model
Model ID of the model providing the output


Downstream model
Model ID of the model receiving the input


Connection type
From the types defined in Section 5.1


Output variable
What the upstream model provides (e.g., routed flow at [gauge], water level at [node])


Input variable
How that output is used by the downstream model (e.g., upstream inflow boundary at node X)


Transfer method
How the output reaches the downstream model: direct file transfer, API call, manual copy, Flode pipeline step


Time offset
Any lag or lead time applied between the upstream output and the downstream input


Manual override
Whether an override point exists; if so, who can authorise and action it


Failure mode
What happens to the downstream model if this connection fails or the upstream model produces no output


Status
Active, Suspended, or Deprecated

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
12.3 5.3 System Diagrams
The Connection Register is the authoritative record of model connections, but a system diagram showing the full cascade is required for every operational catchment or group of connected catchments. The diagram must show each model node, the direction of data flow, the connection type at each link, and any manual override points.
System diagrams are stored in the docs/ directory of the relevant model repository and must be updated whenever the Connection Register is updated. They do not need to be detailed engineering drawings: a clear flowchart identifying each model, its type, and the connections between it is sufficient. The Custodian produces and maintains these diagrams; the Steward reviews them as part of the annual audit if any modifications have been made.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
12.4 5.4 Impact Assessment for Model Changes
Before any change to a model is deployed, the Custodian must consult the Connection Register to identify all downstream models that receive inputs from the model being changed. The impact assessment must consider:

Whether the output format, units, or temporal resolution of the upstream model changes in a way that the downstream model does not expect
Whether the recalibrated or updated upstream model produces materially different outputs under the conditions the downstream models are designed for
Whether any manual override points need to be adjusted
Whether the condition assessment for downstream models needs to be updated to reflect the changed upstream input

For Tier 1 models, the impact assessment is a required step before a pull request is merged and before a new model version is deployed to the operational environment. It must be documented in the run record or change log for the upstream model being updated.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
14.1 7.1 Calibration Records
Every calibrated model version must have a calibration record. This is distinct from and complementary to the run records produced during the calibration process itself.







Field
Description




Model ID and version
The model version produced by this calibration


Calibration period
Start and end dates of the period used for calibration


Events used
List of flood events used, with dates and peak flow or level at key sites


Observed data sources
Gold dataset IDs and versions for all observed data used; rating curve versions noted


Performance metrics
Results at each calibration site: NSE, KGE, FAR, or equivalent; peak timing error; peak magnitude error


Validation period
Start and end dates of the period used for validation


Validation performance
Same metrics as calibration, applied to the validation period


Parameter changes from previous version
What was changed and the justification


Known limitations
Conditions or event types where the calibration is known to perform less well


Calibrated by

Reviewed by
Name of the Steward who reviewed and approved the calibration


Date approved
Date the Steward confirmed the calibration met the required standard

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
section: 14.2 7.2 Performance Thresholds (probably need a better name)
text:
14.2 7.2 Performance Thresholds (probably need a better name)
The Steward defines and maintains performance thresholds for each model type and each key site. These thresholds form part of the condition assessment (Section 4) and the calibration approval process. A calibration that does not meet thresholds at any key site must be reviewed by the Steward before the model version is approved for operational use.
Thresholds are stored in the Model Register alongside each model’s entry and reviewed as part of the annual audit. Where a threshold is relaxed for a specific model or site, the Owner must approve the relaxation and the reason must be recorded.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
15.1 8.1 Promotion to Tier 1
Promotion of a model to Tier 1 operational status requires:

A complete calibration record meeting performance thresholds at all key sites
A condition assessment with a rating of Satisfactory (7-8) or above
All connections to and from the model documented in the Connection Register
A system diagram current and reviewed by the Steward
A handover note or runbook sufficient for another team member to run the model operationally
Owner sign-off

Promotion to Tier 1 does not mean the model will not change. It means that changes to a Tier 1 model follow the full change process including impact assessment, run record, and Steward review before deployment.

title: 6  Flood Model Governance
text:
15.2 8.2 Deprecation
A model is deprecated when it is replaced by a newer version or an alternative model, or if the operational need it served no longer exists. Deprecation requires Owner approval. A deprecated model’s files are retained and its status in the Model Register is set to Deprecated. The previous version is never deleted: it is the record of what produced historical outputs.
Where a deprecated model provided inputs to downstream models, the Connection Register must be updated before deprecation is confirmed and the downstream models’ run records must note the change in upstream input from the date of deprecation.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
8 Purpose
This document sets out the staff training framework for the Forecasting and Warning (F&W) team. It defines what training is required, who must complete it, and how completion is recorded. The framework is structured to ensure that every team member understands the governance obligations relevant to their role, without requiring everyone to cover everything.
Training is organised into four layers: a core that all staff complete; a fundamentals band covering scientific and technical foundations; a cross-cutting section that applies to all modellers regardless of specialism; and specialist tracks for hydrological modelling, hydraulic modelling, R development, and Python and machine learning. A crossover module sits between the hydraulic and Python tracks for staff working with the Flood Modeller API in Python.
Figure 1: Staff training framework structure
The framework has four layers. Each layer builds on the one before it.
The diagram below shows the full structure. Arrows indicate the recommended completion order.
Every team member must complete the core section before starting any specialist track. It covers the governance principles, roles, and structures that underpin all team activity.
These tracks are for graduates who bring scientific knowledge from their degree but are new to the F&W context. The aim is not to teach from scratch but to bridge between general scientific training and the specific methods, tools, and conventions used in operational flood forecasting. Each section below frames what to focus on and points to the best external resources for doing so.
This section is required for all staff who work with flood models in any capacity. It covers the shared governance requirements that apply regardless of whether a model is hydrological, hydraulic, or data-driven. It also covers black box models specifically, as these carry governance risks that require all modellers to understand their limitations.
Staff complete the track or tracks that match their day-to-day work. Unlike the fundamentals, which build conceptual grounding, the specialist tracks are about operational competence: knowing the specific tools, conventions, and governance requirements used in this team’s pipelines.
The table below sets out the minimum training required for each role. Where a team member holds multiple roles (for example, Custodian on an R tool and Custodian on a flood model), they must complete the requirements for each.
Training completion is recorded using the sign-off forms in Appendix A. A separate form exists for each track. The Steward is responsible for keeping completed forms and for confirming that custodians on Tier 1 assets have completed the required training before being listed on the register.
Each form below covers one training section. The completing staff member signs (or dates) the ‘Completed’ column for each item. The verifying colleague (Steward or Delegated Steward) signs the ‘Verified by’ column.
Store completed forms in: docs/training/[StaffName][Track][Year].docx

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
10.1 2.1 Topics covered

The Data and Digital Asset Governance Framework: purpose, scope, and where it sits alongside other organisational policies
The Owner, Steward, and Custodian role structure: what each role does, grade requirements, and how delegation works
The tier system: Tier 1 operational, Tier 2 analytical, and Tier 3 experimental assets; what each means in practice
