title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
10.2 2.2 Expected outcome
On completing the core section, a team member should be able to identify the Owner, Steward, and Custodian for any asset they work with; understand what tier their work falls under; know where assets must be stored; and understand why the governance framework exists in terms of real operational consequences.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
11.1 3.1 Hydrology fundamentals
Recommended for: all staff working with hydrological models, hydrometric data, or ML development. Also useful background for hydraulic modellers working closely with PDM-derived inflow boundaries.
The focus here is on applied catchment hydrology at the scale of UK river systems: how rainfall becomes runoff, how that runoff is routed through a catchment, how it is measured, and how model performance is assessed. University hydrology courses often cover global or theoretical perspectives; the resources below ground these concepts in the practical and computational methods used in UK operational forecasting.

11.1.1 Key concepts to build

Catchment water balance and the main controls on runoff generation: soil moisture, antecedent conditions, infiltration, and the distinction between overland flow and subsurface pathways
Hydrograph anatomy: rising limb, peak, recession; what shape tells you about a catchment; how antecedent conditions shift the response
Unit hydrograph theory and its limitations; why PDM uses a more physically-based approach
Flow routing: lag and attenuation through a channel; the difference between hydrological and hydraulic routing
Evapotranspiration: potential versus actual ET; the Penman-Monteith approach; why it matters for PDM calibration
Model performance metrics: NSE, KGE, FAR, and RMSE; what good values look like; why certain metrics are used over others, e.g. KGE is preferred over NSE for peak flows
Catchment descriptors: BFI, area, mean elevation, soil type, land cover; where they come from (FEH, HOST classification) and how they are useful in a real time context



11.1.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Beven, K. (2012). Rainfall-Runoff Modelling: The Primer. 2nd ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
The standard reference for conceptual and physical rainfall-runoff models. Chapter 2 on catchment water balance and Chapter 5 on PDM-type models are directly relevant. Read alongside PDM documentation.


Peel, M.C. & McMahon, T.A. (2020). Hydrological processes. Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews. doi:10.1002/wat2.1461
A concise overview of modern catchment hydrology. Useful for grounding the more theoretical concepts from Beven in current practice.


Flood Estimation Handbook (FEH) online service: fehweb.ceh.ac.uk
The UK standard for flood frequency estimation. Relevant for understanding catchment descriptors (BFIHOST, PROPWET, URBEXT) that appear in PDM parameter sets and ML feature tables.


Kling, H. et al. (2012). Runoff conditions in the upper Danube basin. Journal of Hydrology. doi:10.1016/j.jhydrol.2012.01.011
The paper that defines KGE. Short and readable. Understand why KGE decomposes NSE into correlation, bias, and variability components, and when this matters for calibration.


NRFA (National River Flow Archive): nrfa.ceh.ac.uk
Explore real UK flow records, catchment descriptors, and hydrograph shapes. Browsing gauges you will work with is one of the best ways to build intuition for catchment response.


Bell, V.A. et al. (2007). Development of a high resolution grid-based river flow model for use with regional climate model output. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences. doi:10.5194/hess-11-532-2007
Background on grid-based hydrological modelling in a UK operational context. Useful for understanding how the national modelling infrastructure relates to catchment-scale work.









F&W context note The PDM (Probability Distributed Model) is the team’s primary rainfall-runoff tool. Its parameter sets encode the catchment characteristics above. When you read about soil moisture storage capacity or drainage parameters in a PDM calibration record, the concepts above are what those parameters represent. The goal of reading this material is to be able to look at a parameter set and understand what it is saying about the catchment, not just treat it as a set of numbers to store.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
11.2 3.2 Hydraulics fundamentals
Recommended for: all FMP users. Also useful for Python developers working with FMP API outputs who need to interpret model results rather than just pass files between systems.
Most graduates have covered fluid mechanics to some degree. The focus here is specifically on open-channel flow and computational hydraulics: the assumptions underlying 1D and 2D solvers, how floodplains are represented, and where models break down. The operational context matters: understanding model limitations is as important as understanding what the model computes.

11.2.1 Key concepts to build

Continuity and momentum: the Saint-Venant equations and what simplifications the 1D diffusion wave and kinematic wave approaches make, and when those simplifications are acceptable
Critical flow, Froude number, and why transitions between subcritical and supercritical flow cause solver instability in 1D schemes
Cross-section representation in 1D models: how a river cross-section is surveyed, stored in a DAT file, and used to compute conveyance; the role of roughness coefficients (Manning’s n)
Floodplain representation: how 1D models use flood storage cells or ISIS/FMP pseudo-2D structures; where this breaks down compared to a full 2D solution
Boundary conditions in hydraulic models: upstream inflow hydrographs, downstream rating curves or tidal boundaries, lateral inflows; how errors in boundaries propagate through the model
Model calibration and validation: roughness adjustment as the primary calibration parameter; NSE and water level error as performance metrics; the distinction between well-calibrated and well-conditioned
2D shallow water equations: depth-averaged flow; when to use a 2D domain rather than 1D; computational cost trade-offs
Linked 1D-2D modelling: what the link does, how flow transfers between the 1D channel and the 2D floodplain domain, and what can go wrong at the interface



11.2.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Cunge, J.A., Holly, F.M. & Verwey, A. (1980). Practical Aspects of Computational River Hydraulics. Pitman.
The foundational text for 1D computational hydraulics. Chapters 2-4 on the Saint-Venant equations and their numerical solution are the theoretical basis for FMP’s 1D solver. Dense but worth the effort for anyone who will be diagnosing model instabilities.


Bates, P.D., Horritt, M.S. & Fewtrell, T.J. (2010). A simple inertial formulation of the shallow water equations for efficient 2D flood inundation modelling. Journal of Hydrology. doi:10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.03.027
Introduces the LISFLOOD-FP approach underlying many 2D solvers. Read for intuition about what a 2D shallow water solver is doing and where diffusion-wave approximations are valid.


Flood Modeller Pro documentation: floodmodeller.com/support
The FMP user manual and technical reference. Before using the software, read the sections on 1D scheme types (ISIS units), boundary conditions, and the 2D solver options. This is the operational reference, not a textbook.


Environment Agency (2012). Coastal Flood Boundary Conditions for the UK. Technical Report.
Background on the tidal boundary conditions used at the downstream end of estuarine FMP models. Relevant for any model that is tidally influenced.


Hunter, N.M. et al. (2007). Benchmarking 2D hydraulic models for urban flood simulations. Proceedings of the ICE - Water Management. doi:10.1680/wama.2007.160.1.13
A comparison of 2D model performance across test cases. Useful for understanding what 2D models do well and poorly, and what that means for interpreting results.


Horritt, M.S. & Bates, P.D. (2002). Evaluation of 1D and 2D numerical models for predicting river flood inundation. Journal of Hydrology. doi:10.1016/S0022-1694(02)00121-X
Classic comparison of 1D versus 2D performance for floodplain inundation.









F&W context note FMP models in the operational system are driven by PDM outputs as upstream boundary conditions. This means an error in the PDM (wrong parameter set, stale calibration) propagates directly into the hydraulic model’s results. When you are diagnosing a forecast that looks wrong, the first question is often whether the issue is in the hydraulic model or in the boundary conditions it received. Understanding both ends of the pipeline is what makes this team’s work different from standalone hydraulic modelling applied in other parts of the business.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
11.3 3.3 Data and coding fundamentals
Recommended for: all staff who will write, review, or run code. Provides the grounding for both the R and Python specialist tracks.
Most science graduates have some programming experience but have rarely worked in a team codebase with version control, dependency management, and code review as standard practice. The resources here focus on those collaborative and reproducibility practices, not on learning to program from scratch.

11.3.1 Key concepts to build

Git fundamentals: commits as snapshots, branches as parallel lines of work, pull requests as the review gateway; what a merge conflict is and how to resolve one
Why version control matters in operational forecasting: a script that produced a forecast six months ago must be reproducible; that requires knowing exactly which version of the code and which package versions were used
Tabular data concepts: the difference between long and wide format; what a join is; what missing values represent and why treating them carelessly causes silent errors
File formats: why Parquet is used instead of CSV for large datasets; what columnar storage means for query performance; when JSON is appropriate
Package management: why pinning package versions matters; what a lockfile does; the difference between a development dependency and a runtime dependency
Code review: what a reviewer is looking for (correctness, clarity, test coverage, governance compliance); how to give feedback that is specific and actionable; how to receive it
Functions and modularity: why a 500-line script is harder to maintain than ten 50-line functions; what a pure function is; why side effects in functions are dangerous in a pipeline context



11.3.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Happy Git and GitHub for the useR: happygitwithr.com (Bryan, J.)
The clearest practical introduction to Git for data scientists. Even if you will primarily use Python, read chapters 1-20 for the concepts. The R-specific parts are optional at this stage.


Pro Git (free): git-scm.com/book
The comprehensive Git reference. Chapters 1-3 cover everything needed for day-to-day use. Chapter 3 on branching is particularly important for understanding the team’s workflow.


Wickham, H. (2019). Advanced R, 2nd ed. (free): adv-r.hadley.nz – Chapter 2: Names and values; Chapter 6: Functions
Even for non-R users, chapters 2 and 6 give a clear conceptual model of how functions and environments work. The ideas transfer directly to Python.


Wilson, G. et al. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510
A practical manifesto for reproducible scientific code. Read the sections on project organisation, keeping track of changes, and making code readable. Maps directly to the team’s governance requirements.


Apache Arrow / Parquet overview: arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html
A readable explanation of columnar storage and why it matters. Understanding this makes the Bronze store’s Parquet structure and partitioning strategy make sense rather than feel arbitrary.


The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT): missing.csail.mit.edu
Short video lectures on shell tools, Git, and editors. Particularly useful if command-line work feels unfamiliar. The Git lecture is one of the best short introductions available.









F&W context note The team uses R and Python in different parts of the pipeline. R (via the reach.* packages) handles data ingestion, quality control, ensemble processing, and visualisation. Python handles the Flood Modeller API, ML training pipelines, and the Databricks environment. The two connect via Parquet files: R writes to the Bronze/Silver/Gold store; Python reads from it. Understanding both languages at a conceptual level, even if you only write in one, makes it much easier to debug problems at the boundary between them.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
12.1 4.1 Model register and model IDs

What the Model Register is and how it differs from the Tool Register
The model ID convention: [CatchmentID][ModelType][Version] and what each element means
When a model must be entered in the register: at first use in a formal output or when shared with another team member
What fields must be completed and who is responsible for keeping them current

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
12.2 4.2 Model configuration
Model configuration covers the decisions made in setting up a model for a run: the input data used, the boundary conditions applied, and any overrides or adjustments made. These decisions must be documented so that any output can be reproduced and audited.

Run records: what must be recorded for every formal model run, including model ID and version, input data IDs, boundary condition datasets, software version, and any overrides applied
Boundary conditions: what they are, the main types (upstream inflow, tidal, lateral inflow, reservoir rules, gate settings), and what governance applies to each
Calibration and validation records: what must be documented, the distinction between calibration and validation, and what performance thresholds are required before a model can be promoted to Tier 1
Impact assessment for model changes: how to identify downstream models affected by a change before deploying it

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
12.3 4.3 Model condition
Model condition is a structured assessment of how fit for purpose a model is at a given point. It is distinct from whether a model is currently producing acceptable outputs – a model can be performing within tolerance while being in poor condition.

What condition assessment covers: data currency, structural integrity, calibration currency, software currency, and documentation completeness
Condition scoring: the 0-10 scale and what the descriptive ratings (Good, Acceptable, Poor, Critical) mean operationally
Review schedules: standard annual reviews and triggered reviews following significant events
How condition propagates: a poor-condition upstream model passes uncertainty to all downstream models, regardless of their own condition score

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
12.4 4.4 Model connections and cascading systems

What the Connection Register is and why it exists
Connection types: how PDM outputs drive FMP models, how FMP models drive downstream FMP models, and where black box models fit
System diagrams: what they must show and who maintains them
Manual override points: what they are, who can authorise their use, and what must be recorded when they are used
Failure modes: what happens to downstream models when an upstream connection fails

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
12.5 4.5 Black box models
Black box models relate inputs directly to outputs without representing physical processes in between. This includes transfer function models and, in the team’s development pipeline, LSTM neural network models. Because their internal workings are not physically interpretable, they carry specific governance risks.

What distinguishes a black box model from a physically-based model, and what governance risks this creates
Why performance degradation in a black box model may not be apparent until a significant event occurs
The requirement for a documented training dataset and the difference between training data and operational input data
Why all black box models used in operational forecasting are Tier 1 assets by default
Condition assessment for black box models: why it matters more than for physically-based models and how it is carried out
Deprecation and handover: what must be recorded when a black box model is replaced by a newer ML model

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
13.1 5.1 Hydrological modelling
For staff developing, maintaining, or running PDM configurations and working with hydrometric data. Complete the hydrology fundamentals section (3.1) before starting this track.

13.1.1 PDM models
The PDM is a conceptual rainfall-runoff model that transforms rainfall and potential evapotranspiration inputs into catchment runoff. In the team’s system, PDM outputs are the primary upstream inflow boundary for FMP hydraulic models. A poorly calibrated PDM directly degrades every downstream model that relies on its output.

PDM model structure: the soil moisture storage component, the groundwater recharge component, and the routing module; what each parameter controls physically
Parameter sets as versioned assets: why two analysts calibrating the same catchment on different data periods can produce materially different parameter sets; why this makes version control and calibration records non-negotiable
Naming and storage: the required naming convention, the prohibition on local machine storage, and what a complete parameter set repository entry looks like
Calibration records: what must be documented – calibration period, input data IDs and versions, events used, performance metrics (NSE, KGE, volume error), and known limitations
How PDM outputs become FMP boundary conditions: the format, temporal resolution, and what happens when a PDM run produces negative flows or physically implausible values



13.1.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Moore, R.J. (2007). The PDM rainfall-runoff model. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences. doi:10.5194/hess-11-483-2007
The primary reference for the PDM. Read this before attempting to interpret or adjust a parameter set. Focus on the soil moisture storage function and how the shape parameter controls the distribution of storage capacity across the catchment.


PDM user manual (internal): available from the Steward
Covers the software interface, input file formats, parameter definitions, and output structure. Essential reading before running a calibration. Pay particular attention to the section on parameter sensitivity.


Wagener, T. et al. (2004). Rainfall-Runoff Modelling in Hydrology. Wiley.
A broader treatment of conceptual model calibration and uncertainty. Chapter 4 on parameter estimation and Chapter 6 on performance assessment directly support PDM calibration practice.





13.1.3 Hydrometric data
The Bronze-to-Gold pipeline is the team’s mechanism for moving raw gauge data into a form that is fit for model calibration and ML training. Understanding it from end to end is essential before using any data for a formal purpose.

Data sources: the EA Hydrology Data Explorer (HDE) API and WISKI; what each provides; the difference between near-real-time telemetry data and quality-controlled archive data
Bronze: raw ingestion from the HDE API; the partitioned Parquet store structure (site_id, year); why Bronze is immutable and what that means in practice if you find an error
Silver: quality control; what the supplier quality flags and q-codes mean; what manual review adds beyond automated flagging; the completeness threshold for Silver promotion
Gold: formal approval for a named purpose; what a Gold derivation record must contain; who may approve Gold data; why only Gold data may be used in Tier 1 model runs or ML training promoted to operational use
Q-FAIR compliance: what Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable mean for a Gold dataset in this context; what the quality gate adds beyond FAIR



13.1.4 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Environment Agency Hydrology Data Explorer: environment.data.gov.uk/hydrology
Browse the gauges the team works with. Understand the data fields returned by the API: dateTime, value, completeness, quality, and qcode. This is the source of everything in the Bronze store.


WMO (2010). Manual on Stream Gauging. WMO-No. 1044.
The international standard for hydrometric practice. Volume I chapters on discharge measurement and rating curves give the physical basis for the data the team ingests. Helps interpret quality flags sensibly rather than mechanically.


Marsh, T. & Hannaford, J. (2008). UK Hydrometric Register. Centre for Ecology and Hydrology.
Background on the UK gauging network, instrumentation types, and known data quality issues by gauge type. Useful context for understanding why some gauges have persistent quality problems.


reach.io package documentation (internal): available in docs/reach.io/
The team’s R package for reading from and writing to the Bronze/Silver/Gold store. Read the function reference for ingest_bronze(), promote_silver(), and approve_gold() before handling any data in the pipeline.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
13.2 5.2 Hydraulic modelling
For staff developing, maintaining, or running FMP models. Complete the hydraulics fundamentals section (3.2) before starting this track.

13.2.1 FMP governance
FMP models are binary files. Unlike R or Python scripts, you cannot easily read a diff of what changed between two versions. This makes formal version control and run records the only reliable mechanism for tracing what model produced what output.

Folder structure: the required directory layout for every FMP project; why deviating from it breaks the automated tools that read model files
File naming: the model ID convention [CatchmentID][ModelType][Version]; how version numbers increment at patch, minor, and major levels; what constitutes a major change requiring Owner sign-off
Version control for binary files: using Git LFS or the agreed repository structure for FMP project files; how to tag a version used in a formal output so it can be recovered; the prohibition on local-only storage
Run records: completing every required field; the difference between a casual test run and a formal output; what triggers the obligation to complete a run record



13.2.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Flood Modeller Pro user manual: floodmodeller.com/support
The primary reference. Before working on any model, read the sections covering the unit types you will encounter (ISIS River, ISIS Spill, ISIS Reservoir, 2D domain). The reference manual section on each unit explains what each parameter does.


Flood Modeller Pro worked examples (included with software installation)
Work through the 1D steady-state and 1D unsteady examples before touching a live model. The unsteady examples are the most relevant to operational forecasting.


Horritt, M.S. & Bates, P.D. (2002) – see Section 3.2 resources
Re-read with operational intent: when you are deciding options for a new model build, this paper is the reference for that decision.


Environment Agency (2010). Flood risk assessment: the requirements for FRMPs. Technical guidance.
Context for how flood models are used in a regulatory and operational setting in England. Useful background for understanding why model condition and documentation standards are not just bureaucracy.





13.2.3 1D, 2D, and linked configurations
Information on 2D and linked configurations have been included due to their use in modelled rating curve development. Though for most day-to-day forecast modelling tasks, 1D modelling will suffice.

Choosing a scheme: the criteria for 1D (well-defined channel, limited floodplain complexity), 2D (significant floodplain flow paths, urban areas), and linked (channel + complex floodplain); how computational cost scales
GXY files: the reach centreline format; how GXY geometry is used for spatial referencing and for the reach.* package’s spatial tools
DAT files: node coordinates and cross-section data; how to read a DAT file and what each section header means; the label format used in the team’s model register
Running a model: steady-state versus unsteady; what a warm-up period is and why it matters for operational runs; what to check in the output before trusting results
Diagnosing instabilities: what negative flow, mass balance errors, and numerical blowup look like in FMP output; the common causes and how to address them without breaking the calibration



13.2.4 Crossover module: FMP API scripting
Required for any staff member running FMP models via Python scripts rather than the GUI, regardless of primary track. Complete this in conjunction with the Python governance track (5.4).

What the Flood Modeller API exposes: how to open a model, set boundary conditions programmatically, run the solver, and read outputs; the Python object model for FMP projects
Tier 1 tool obligations: a Python script that runs an operational FMP model is a Tier 1 tool; it requires poetry for dependency management, Git version control, a run record for each execution, 70% test coverage, and a disaster recovery runbook
How tool and model governance interact: the Model Register records the model version; the Tool Register records the script version; a run record must reference both
Testing FMP orchestration scripts: what to test (boundary condition setting, output reading, error handling) and what not to test (the FMP solver itself)



13.2.5 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Flood Modeller Pro API documentation: floodmodeller.com/api
The primary reference for the Python API. Read the quickstart guide and the worked examples for running unsteady simulations. The API wraps the same solver as the GUI, so GUI knowledge transfers directly.


Flood Modeller API GitHub repository: github.com/People-Places-Solutions/floodmodeller-api
The source code and issue tracker for the open-source API package. Useful for understanding what the API does under the hood and for reporting bugs.

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
13.3 5.3 R development
For staff writing, maintaining, or reviewing R code. Complete the data and coding fundamentals section (3.3) before starting this track.

13.3.1 R governance
The R Tool Governance document sets the standards. This track is about being able to work within those standards in practice, not just knowing they exist.

Tool tier classification in R: assess a tool by asking who is affected if it fails – Tier 1 if the answer is an operational forecast; Tier 2 if the answer is an analytical output; Tier 3 if it is experimental
renv in practice: renv::init() when starting a new project; renv::snapshot() before every commit that changes a package; renv::restore() when setting up a colleague’s project; what to do when the lockfile and installed packages diverge
The prohibition on dplyr and tidyverse in team tools: this is a hard rule, not a preference. data.table is faster, has a stable API, and reduces dependencies. You may use tidyverse in personal exploration but never in shared tools
The code review process: how to open a pull request; what the reviewer checks (correctness, test coverage, documentation, governance header, dependency changes); what blocks a merge



13.3.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




R Tool Governance document (internal)
Read in full before writing any shared R code. The sections on tool tiers, code review requirements by tier, and the renv workflow are the most operationally important.


data.table wiki: rdatatable.gitlab.io/data.table
The authoritative reference for data.table. The ‘Getting started’ vignettes cover the DT[i, j, by] syntax. The ‘Reference semantics’ vignette explains why modifying by reference matters for performance. Read before writing any data manipulation code.


Fastverse documentation: fastverse.github.io/fastverse
Overview of the fastverse ecosystem (data.table, collapse, kit). Understand what each package contributes and when to reach for collapse versus data.table.


R Packages, 2nd ed. (free): r-pkgs.org (Wickham & Bryan)
The standard reference for R package development. Read chapters on package structure, documentation (roxygen2), and testing (testthat) before contributing to the reach.* packages.


testthat documentation: testthat.r-lib.org
Read the ‘Testing basics’ article before writing any tests. Understand the difference between expect_equal, expect_identical, and expect_error; how to structure test files; and how test_that() groups related expectations.


Happy Git with R: happygitwithr.com (Bryan)
If the Git workflow is new, work through chapters 1-20. The sections on branching and pull requests are directly relevant to the team’s review process.





13.3.3 The flode (reach.*) package suite
All reusable R code goes into the reach.* packages – these are consolidated into flode. Understanding the package structure before writing code prevents duplication and keeps the codebase coherent.

reach.io: data ingestion and the Parquet store; reading from and writing to the Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers; the HDE API connector; Arrow dataset handling
reach.hydro: hydrological calculations; PDM utilities; flow statistics; catchment descriptor access
reach.ensemble: ensemble forecast processing; probability of exceedance calculations; ensemble spread metrics
reach.validate: model performance metrics (NSE, KGE, FAR, RMSE); calibration assessment utilities; event identification
reach.viz: standardised visualisation functions; hydrograph plotting; ensemble fan charts; map utilities using sf and leaflet
reach.utils: shared utilities used across packages; date/time handling; logging via cli; configuration helpers



13.3.4 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




reach.* package documentation (internal): available in docs/reach.*/
Read the README for each package you will contribute to before writing code. The function register lists what exists; duplicate functions are a maintenance burden.


data.table cheat sheet: community resource at github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/wiki
A quick reference for common operations. Keep it open while writing data manipulation code until the syntax is second nature.


Arrow R package documentation: arrow.apache.org/docs/r
Read the ‘Working with Arrow Datasets’ article to understand how Arrow handles partitioned Parquet stores. This is what reach.io uses under the hood for the Bronze store.


collapse package documentation: sebkrantz.github.io/collapse
Reference for the collapse package. Focus on the fmutate(), fgroup_by(), and fsummarise() functions, which replace dplyr equivalents in the fastverse workflow.





13.3.5 Tier 1 tool standards
*Currently no R tools are implemented in **supporting live operational forecasting.*
Any R tool in the operational forecast chain is Tier 1 from the moment it is promoted. The additional requirements beyond standard development practice are:

Test coverage: 70% line coverage measured by covr; the CI pipeline enforces this and blocks merges if the threshold is not met; coverage reports are generated on every pull request
Disaster recovery runbooks: a runbook documents what to do if the tool fails during an operational event; it must specify the manual workaround, who to contact, and how long the fallback is viable
Handover notes: required when a Custodian changes; covers the tool’s purpose, known quirks, technical debt, open issues, and scheduled maintenance; stored in docs/ alongside the code
Senior reviewer confirmation: before a team member is listed as Custodian on a Tier 1 tool, a senior reviewer must confirm in writing that they have demonstrated competence to maintain it

title: 7  Staff Training Framework
text:
13.4 5.4 Python and machine learning
For staff writing Python tools or working in the AI/ML development environment. Complete the data and coding fundamentals section (3.3) before starting this track. The hydrology fundamentals (3.1) are also recommended before working on the LSTM pipelines.

13.4.1 Python governance
The Python Tool Governance document mirrors the R governance document in structure. The key operational differences are the dependency management tool (poetry rather than renv), the deployment environment (Databricks as well as local execution), and the strict training/inference separation requirement.

poetry in practice: poetry new or poetry init to start a project; poetry add  to add dependencies (never pip install directly in a managed project); poetry install when setting up a colleague’s project; poetry shell to activate the environment; committing poetry.lock with every dependency change
Training and inference separation: the training pipeline and the inference pipeline must be in separate scripts with no shared mutable state; this is a governance requirement, not just a design preference; the reason is auditability – the Steward must be able to confirm which training run produced the deployed model
Tool tier classification: the same criteria as R; a Python script that runs operational inference is Tier 1 from the moment it is deployed, regardless of how experimental the development felt
Code review: the same process as R; reviewers additionally check that training and inference are separated, that MLflow logging is complete, and that the Gold data requirement is met



13.4.2 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Python Tool Governance document (internal): available from the Steward
Read in full before writing any shared Python code. The sections on poetry, training/inference separation, and Tier 1 obligations are the most operationally important.


Poetry documentation: python-poetry.org/docs
Read ‘Basic usage’ and ‘Managing dependencies’ before starting any project. The section on dependency groups is relevant for separating development and runtime dependencies.


Real Python – Python Virtual Environments Primer: realpython.com/python-virtual-environments-a-primer
Understand what a virtual environment is and why it exists before using poetry. Poetry automates this, but knowing what it is doing prevents confusion when something goes wrong.


MLflow documentation: mlflow.org/docs/latest
Read the ‘Tracking’ and ‘Models’ sections. Understand how experiments, runs, parameters, metrics, and artefacts relate to each other. This is the logging infrastructure for all ML work in the team.


Databricks documentation – Unity Catalog: docs.databricks.com/en/data-governance/unity-catalog
Read the overview and the section on catalogs, schemas, and tables. Unity Catalog is how data is governed inside Databricks; understanding its structure is necessary before reading from or writing to the DASH platform.





13.4.3 The AI/ML test environment
ML development in the team happens in a staged environment on DEFRA’s DASH Databricks platform. The stages exist to separate experimental work from anything that could affect operational outputs.

Stage 1 – canned datasets: development uses CAMELS-GB v2 and UK-Flow15; no EA operational data; the goal is to validate the pipeline architecture before touching real data
Stage 2 – EA data integration: Silver-tier hydrometric data from the Bronze/Silver/Gold store; Steward approval required; data IDs must be logged to MLflow
Stage 3 – pseudo-operational testing: Gold-tier data; real-time feed integration; results assessed against existing black box models on the same events before any promotion decision
Progression between stages is evidence-led: a stage is complete when the Steward agrees the evidence warrants moving on, not when a calendar date is reached
MLflow logging requirements: every experiment run must log the model architecture, all hyperparameters, the training data ID and version, validation metrics (NSE, KGE on held-out events), and the ONNX model artefact



13.4.4 Recommended resources







Resource
What to take from it




Kratzert, F. et al. (2018). Rainfall-runoff modelling using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences. doi:10.5194/hess-22-6005-2018
The paper that established LSTMs as serious tools for rainfall-runoff modelling. Read before writing any LSTM code. Understand what the model is learning and why LSTM architecture suits sequential hydrological data.


Kratzert, F. et al. (2019). Towards learning universal, regional, and local hydrological behaviors via machine learning applied to large-sample datasets. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences. doi:10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019
The follow-up paper introducing static catchment attributes as LSTM inputs (equivalent to the team’s BFI, area, elevation features). Read to understand why static attributes improve regionalisation.


CAMELS-GB dataset documentation: doi.org/10.5285/8344e4f3-d2ea-44f5-8afa-86d2987543a9
The Stage 1 training dataset. Read the dataset documentation to understand what attributes are included and how they align with the team’s feature engineering pipeline.


PyTorch documentation – nn.LSTM: pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html
The reference for the LSTM implementation used in the training pipeline. Understand the input shape (sequence_length, batch_size, input_size) before writing any training code – shape errors are the most common source of bugs.


MLflow Python API reference: mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api
Reference for mlflow.log_param(), mlflow.log_metric(), mlflow.log_artifact(), and mlflow.pytorch.log_model(). All four are required in every training run.


ONNX documentation: onnx.ai/onnx/intro
Background on the ONNX model format used for archiving Tier 1 models. Read the overview and the Python export guide. ONNX export is required before any model can be promoted to Tier 1.





13.4.5 LSTM pipelines
The LSTM pipeline has three components: feature engineering, training, and inference. Each is a separate script. The governance requirement for separation means they must not share mutable state or call each other at runtime.

Feature engineering: constructing the input tensors from Silver or Gold hydrometric time series; sequence length and lookback window selection; normalisation using training-set statistics only (never the full dataset, to prevent data leakage); fixed random seeds for reproducible train/test splits
Static catchment attributes: BFI, catchment area, mean elevation, soil type, land cover, and gauge coordinates; loaded from the fw_gold Parquet store; concatenated with dynamic inputs at training time, not baked into the sequence
Training pipeline: LSTM architecture definition; training loop with early stopping; validation on held-out events; hyperparameter logging to MLflow; ONNX export on completion
Inference pipeline: loading the promoted LSTM from the MLflow registry; running against incoming Silver data; the inference script must not import from the training script
Model handover: when an LSTM replaces an existing black box model, the retiring model’s Tool Register entry is set to Deprecated with a reference to the replacing model’s MLflow run ID; the Connection Register is updated to reflect the new upstream model

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Full glossary






Term
Definition




Asset
Any data, model file, code tool, or digital resource the team creates or relies on


Flood Modeller Pro (FMP)
Hydraulic modelling software used for 1D/2D flood simulation


PDM
Probability Distributed Model: a conceptual rainfall-runoff model


Flode
The team’s internal R package (Flood Operations Development Environment)


Tier 1 / 2 / 3
Asset classification by operational criticality. Tier 1 = live forecasting, Tier 2 = analytical, Tier 3 = experimental


Semantic versioning
Version numbering system: Major.Minor.Patch (e.g. 2.1.0). MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new functionality, PATCH = bug fix


Metadata
Information describing a dataset or model: what it is, where it came from, when it was created


Calibration
The process of adjusting model parameters so outputs match observed data


Tool Register
A version-controlled record of all code tools with ownership, tier, and status


Model Register
A version-controlled record of all flood models with ownership, tier, condition rating, and connections


Connection Register
A version-controlled record of all active connections between models in the team’s operational system


Hydrometric Data Register
The single consolidated record for all Bronze, Silver, and Gold datasets: provenance, QC records, and derivation records in one table


NSE / KGE / FAR
Common hydrological model performance metrics: Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency, Kling-Gupta Efficiency, False Alarm Ratio


renv.lock / poetry.lock
Dependency lockfiles that pin exact package versions for reproducibility; renv for R, poetry for Python


CI
Continuous Integration: automated checks (tests, linting) that run on every code change


Data Owner
As defined in the Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2023): a senior individual with dedicated accountability for a logical grouping of data and in-depth knowledge of the overall business strategy in their data remit


Data Steward
As defined in the Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2023): an operational expert responsible for day-to-day activities supporting the governance decisions made by Data Owners


Delegated Steward
A practitioner to whom the Steward delegates hands-on technical governance work. The delegation recognises that G7 Stewards are often people managers whose strengths lie in oversight and decision-making rather than technical depth; the Delegated Steward brings the domain expertise to carry out the work: assessing code quality, reviewing model condition, evaluating data pipelines, conducting annual Tier 1 audits, and producing corrective action plans. Typically at G6 grade. Delegation does not transfer accountability: the Steward remains responsible for all decisions. Defined in the Governance Framework Role Summary table.


Data Custodian
As defined in the Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2023): an individual responsible for capturing, storing, and disposing of data in line with the Data Owner’s requirements


Information Asset Owner (IAO)
A senior individual accountable for the security, content, quality, and distribution of an information asset (typically a database or IT system). Defined in Cabinet Office guidance (updated October 2025). See Section 2.3.6


Information Asset Manager (IAM)
A delegated role working on behalf of the IAO, with regular responsibility for the proper management of information in their business area


Data catalogue
A maintained record of agreed data definitions, entities, and attributes used across the team. See Section 2.8


Data lineage
The documented chain showing where data came from, how it was transformed, and where it flows to


Bronze
The first tier of the medallion framework. Raw, unmodified data exactly as received from the supplier


Silver
The second tier. Quality-controlled data with flags applied and QC decisions documented


Gold
The third tier. Formally approved analysis-ready products derived from Silver data. Includes aggregated statistics, calibration inputs, and ML training sets


Provenance
The documented origin and history of a dataset: where it came from, when, how it was received, and what has been done to it


Rating curve
The relationship between water level (stage) and flow (discharge) at a gauging station, used to derive flow from level measurements


Gap-filling
Estimating values for missing time periods in a dataset using a documented method


Quality flag
A code attached to each data value indicating its quality status (Good, Estimated, Suspect, Rejected, No data, Below detection)


Flatline
A sequence of identical repeated values in a time series, typically indicating a sensor or telemetry malfunction


Medallion framework
A data architecture pattern organising data into tiers of increasing quality and fitness for purpose. Adapted here for hydrological data management


Hydrometric
Relating to the measurement of water: flows, levels, rainfall, and related variables


NRFA
National River Flow Archive: the UK’s national repository of river flow data


Datum
The vertical reference level to which water level measurements are made


Parquet
A columnar file format used as the standard storage format for all hydrometric datasets. Supports typed columns, compression, and efficient partial reads


Delta Lake
A storage layer built on Parquet that adds transactions, schema enforcement, and time-travel to tables in Databricks. Used for Bronze and Silver stores in DASH


Q-FAIR
Quality, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable: the Defra data standards aims that this framework implements by design


DPIA
Data Protection Impact Assessment: required where processing of personal data may result in high risk to individuals


Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
UK legislation governing data use, access, and sharing; referenced in updated IAO guidance


CDDO
Central Digital and Data Office: the government body responsible for the Data Ownership Model


Conventional Commits
A commit message convention: <type>(<scope>): <description>. Permitted types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore


fastverse
A suite of high-performance R packages (including data.table) that is the team’s default over the tidyverse


polars
The team’s default Python data manipulation library, preferred over pandas for typed, high-performance tabular operations


ONNX
Open Neural Network Exchange: the preferred format for archiving trained ML models intended for long-term operational use


Black Box model
A data-driven model that relates inputs directly to outputs without representing physical processes; includes neural network and transfer function models


Condition rating
A numerical score (0–10) produced by a model condition assessment, mapped to a descriptive rating from Critical to Good


Cascading system
A modelling system where the outputs of one model become the inputs to one or more downstream models


Manual override point
A defined point in a cascading system where an operator can substitute a model output with an observed or manually estimated value


BFI
Base Flow Index: the proportion of river flow derived from groundwater or other slowly varying sources. Ranges from 0 to 1


Static catchment attributes
Time-invariant descriptors of a catchment attached to an ML training set Gold product: area, BFI, elevation, soil type, and land cover


ML training set Gold
A Gold product type holding Silver time series data at native 15-minute resolution with static catchment attributes attached. Distinct from aggregated Gold products

title: Appendix D — Upcoming Changes and Improvements
text:
D.1 Review: Framework Effectiveness Assessment (March 2026)
The following section records a structured review of the document suite against the question: In terms of a data and digital asset governance document, is it effective? Where is it weak?
Reviewer: Claude (AI assistant), prompted by Jonathan Payne, 22 March 2026


D.1.1 Where the Suite is Effective
It addresses its stated problem. The problem statement identifies five concrete risks: no version records, no owners, no audit trail, knowledge loss on turnover, compliance risk. The framework addresses all five with specific, actionable mechanisms. It reads as a document written by someone who has lived with the consequences of not having it.
The tier system is the right design choice. A single governance weight applied to all assets would either over-govern experiments or under-govern operational assets. The three-tier model is proportionate and gives teams permission to be light-touch where it matters less, making them more likely to be rigorous where it matters most.
The hydrometric data chapter is strong. Bronze/Silver/Gold with immutable Bronze, explicit approval gates at each transition, named roles per tier, quarterly reporting, and the principle that data is never overwritten in place. This is well-implemented data governance for a small operational team. The Q-FAIR alignment is embedded structurally, not added as a compliance overlay.
The alignment register is unusually mature. Most team-level governance documents do not trace their requirements back to external policy. This suite identifies nine specific divergences against CDDO, Defra, Cabinet Office, and the National Data Strategy, resolves eight, and documents the justification for the one intentional deviation. That is a strong audit position.
The model condition framework is original and practical. Five-factor scoring (0–10) with defined required actions at each threshold band, including mandatory suspension at Critical, goes beyond what most modelling teams have. The distinction between condition and performance (that a model may still produce acceptable outputs while being in poor condition) is important and well-articulated.



D.1.2 Where the Suite is Weak
The following weaknesses were identified. Each is provisionally assigned a priority for resolution.

D.1.2.1 1. No Implementation Authority






Partially resolved at v1.4



Implementation dates have been set and are now recorded in the parent framework metadata block:

Implementation start: 23 March 2026
Target adoption: 31 March 2026 (end of financial year 2025-26)
Review date: 31 March 2027

All companion document review dates have been updated to reflect the same review cycle.
What still remains: Owner signatures on the approval blocks, and the transition period and register population targets described below. These require Owner engagement and cannot be set unilaterally.


The suite is Draft: For Review. Approval blocks are unsigned and there is no statement of what happens between now and formal adoption. A governance framework without an approval date is a set of suggestions.
What is needed: Owner signatures on the approval blocks, and a transition period for compliance with target dates for populating each register with real asset entries.
Priority: High. Resolves before or at the point of adoption.



D.1.2.2 2. Heavy on “What”, Light on “How”






Partially resolved at v1.4 — Hydrometric Data Register and Tool Register



Hydrometric Data Register: A CSV file maintained by the reach.io R package (github.com/JonPayneEA/reach.io) via write_provenance_record(). A separate Gauge Registry (Parquet) is managed by build_gauge_registry(). Chapter 5 updated.
Tool Register: A generated CSV (tool_register.csv) produced by scripts/build_tool_register.R. The script queries the GitHub API for all repositories in the JonPayneEA organisation and merges each repository’s governance.yml with GitHub metadata. It is not hand-maintained. A governance-template.yml is provided for tool repositories to adopt. The parent framework (Section 7.6) has been updated to reflect this.


The framework defines excellent structures (registers, run records, condition assessments, provenance records) but rarely explains how to create or maintain them in practice. There are no templates, no worked examples, and no indication of where registers live or what format they take.
Specifically: - The Hydrometric Data Register format is now resolved via reach.io (see note above). - The Tool Register format is now resolved via scripts/build_tool_register.R (see note above). - The Model Register physical form is still undefined. - Run records have a 13-field template but no completed example. - The data catalogue is required but its format is left open (“a structured document, a spreadsheet, or a dedicated section”), which in practice means it does not yet exist.
What is needed: Decisions on the Model Register format, a completed run record example, and a data catalogue format decision.
Priority: High.



D.1.2.3 3. Governance Load Not Matched to Capacity
The framework creates a significant and recurring administrative burden:

Quarterly governance summaries from the Steward
Annual Tier 1 audit across all tools, models, and data
Annual condition assessments for all Tier 1 models
Six-monthly access reviews
Monthly Data Quality Issue Log reviews
Annual framework review with Owner sign-off
Annual training verification

For a team where, by the problem statement’s own admission, models currently lack version records and tools lack owners, this is a large step change with no phasing. The risk is that the framework is adopted on paper but not in practice because no one has capacity to run all the review cycles. The MCP server specification (see Appendix E, if adopted) directly addresses this by automating the mechanical portions of many of these obligations.
What is needed: Either a phased compliance timeline that ramps obligations up over 12–18 months as registers are populated and tooling is in place, or explicit acknowledgement that certain obligations (e.g. quarterly summaries, formal condition assessments) do not apply until named assets are registered.
Priority: Medium.



D.1.2.4 4. Cross-Asset Governance at the Boundaries
The framework is strong within individual asset types but weak at the interfaces between them:

Data-to-model: Gold datasets feed Tier 1 models, but there is no mechanism for the data Steward to notify the modelling Steward when a Gold dataset is superseded. The model run record captures the dataset ID used, but there is no trigger to check whether that ID is still the current approved version.
Code-to-model: The Tool Register and Model Register are separate with no cross-referencing. If a Tier 1 R tool depends on the output format of a Tier 1 FMP model, that dependency is not captured anywhere.
Cross-language pipelines: A pipeline that uses both R and Python has no single point of governance accountability.

What is needed: A cross-asset dependency field in each register, or a connection register extended to cover data-to-model and tool-to-model links as well as model-to-model links. The MCP server’s get_connections tool and its unified register backend are the natural implementation vehicle.
Priority: Medium.



D.1.2.5 5. The Accepted File Types Chapter Functioned as a Technical Specification, Not a Governance Document






Resolved at v1.1



The Accepted File Types document has been moved to Appendix E and renamed File Format Reference. Normative requirements are now enforced through the domain governance documents (Hydrometric Data Framework, R Tool Governance, Python Tool Governance) where roles and escalation paths already exist. Format compliance is checked automatically by the fw-governance MCP server check_file_formats tool.


Chapter 2 defined formats but assigned no roles, no enforcement mechanism, no approval gate, and no escalation path. If someone stored data as CSV instead of the required Parquet format, there was no mechanism in the framework for anyone to detect, report, or resolve it. Every other chapter had clear accountability; this one had none.
Resolution: Moved to Appendix E. Normative rules retained in domain chapters. MCP tooling provides automated enforcement.



D.1.2.6 6. Owner Accountability is Structurally Thin
The Owner (Deputy Director) is required to approve Tier 1 promotions, Gold datasets, Poor/Critical model conditions, AI service access, external data sharing, disposal, and the annual framework review. However, the Owner has no required training beyond a brief core module covering governance obligations, no required attendance at any review meeting, and no required interaction with any register or report beyond receiving the quarterly summary.
In practice this creates a risk that the Steward makes real decisions and the Owner rubber-stamps them, which would undermine the governance model the framework depends on. The framework has grade requirements for Steward (G7) and Custodian (any), but no substantive engagement requirements for the Owner beyond sign-off.
What is needed: A brief Owner engagement checklist as part of the annual review, for example confirmation that the Owner has reviewed the quarterly summary, can name the Tier 1 assets in their domain, and has seen the condition ratings for those assets.
Priority: Low. More a maturity improvement than a structural gap.



D.1.2.7 7. Incomplete Sections Undermine Credibility
Several passages in the current draft are working notes rather than governance text:

Chapter 6, §2.3: SEE BLACK BOX DOCUMENT ALAN SENT ME
Chapter 6, §5.1: is this done anywhere? (inline in a table)
Chapter 6, §7.2: (probably need a better name) in a section heading
Chapter 4, §7.1: Python onboarding section marked To be written
Chapter 3, Flode module table: NEEDS MODIFICATION
Multiple review dates remain as [Insert Date]

These are normal in a working draft, but they must be resolved before the document is circulated beyond the immediate authoring team. A Custodian reading the Black Box governance text should not encounter a note referencing a document sent by a colleague.
Priority: High. Resolve before circulation for formal review.



D.1.2.8 8. No Version Control Policy for the Framework Itself






Resolved at v1.4



A Framework Version Control subsection has been added to the Review and Compliance section. It defines three change categories (editorial, substantive, major), the approval route for each, the versioning convention (MAJOR.MINOR with _quarto.yml as master), and the team notification requirement for substantive and major changes.


The framework mandates version control for every other asset type but has no equivalent policy for changes to the governance documents themselves. What happens between annual reviews? Who approves minor corrections? How are changes to companion documents tracked against the parent framework version? The alignment register tracks divergences against external policy but not internal amendments.
What is needed: A brief change control section (perhaps in the Review and Compliance section) covering who may make corrections between reviews, what level of change triggers a version increment, and how changes are communicated to the team.
Priority: Low.

text:
D.2 Proposed Change: Implementation Chapter
Based on the assessment above, a dedicated implementation chapter is proposed as either Chapter 8 or a new companion document. Its purpose would be to bridge the gap between what the framework requires and how a team beginning from the current state can actually put it into practice.
Proposed scope:

Content

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
F Purpose
This appendix is the authoritative reference for which file formats are accepted across F&W team tools and workflows. It covers when each format should be used, how it works, and any important limitations. Where there is a choice between formats, this appendix states the preferred option and the reason for it.
The normative requirements (that Parquet is mandatory at all hydrometric data tiers, that CSV is prohibited in pipelines, that Delta tables are restricted to DASH) are stated and enforced in the domain governance documents that own them. This appendix provides the technical rationale and comparison material to support those requirements.
This document applies to all data files created, stored, or exchanged by F&W Team members, including:
Parquet is the standard format for all tabular data in team tools and pipelines. It is a columnar, compressed, strongly typed binary format. Unlike CSV, it preserves data types exactly and is substantially smaller on disk. It is the native format for the Databricks DASH environment and is readable by R, Python, and Databricks without conversion.
A Delta table is a storage layer built on top of Parquet files, available in the Databricks DASH environment. It adds transactional behaviour to a Parquet-backed table. Delta tables are used for bronze and silver stores in DASH.
Flood Modeller Pro (FMP) uses a set of proprietary binary and text-based files. All must be version-controlled and stored in the agreed folder structure set out in the Flood Model Governance document. Model files must not be held on local machines.
PDM (Probability Distributed Model) converts rainfall and potential evapotranspiration into catchment runoff. PDM assets comprise three file types: parameter sets, configuration files, and calibration records.
Parameter sets are sensitive assets. A set calibrated on one data period can produce materially different outputs from a set calibrated on a different period, even for the same catchment. Version control and calibration documentation are not optional.
NetCDF is the required format for gridded spatial outputs, including gridded weather data, rainfall fields, and any raster data that varies over time.
CSV is acceptable only for small exchange files. It is not an acceptable storage or pipeline format for any dataset the team owns or maintains.
Excel is restricted to final stakeholder deliverables and formal reports. It is not an acceptable format for storing, processing, or sharing data within the team’s own pipelines.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
section: H.1 2.1 Why Parquet for time series
text:
H.1 2.1 Why Parquet for time series
Parquet stores data by column rather than by row. A tool that only needs timestamps and flow values from a file with twenty columns loads only those two columns from disk. For long records across hundreds of gauges this makes a material difference to both speed and memory use.
Timestamps are stored as datetime64[ns, UTC], not as strings. Floats are float64 throughout. This prevents silent type errors when the same file is read by different tools or colleagues.
Parquet uses Snappy compression by default, reducing file size by 60-80% compared to equivalent CSV with no data loss.







Property
Detail




Timestamp type
datetime64[ns, UTC] always. Never store timestamps as strings.


Float type
float64 throughout. Do not downcast to float32.


Integer type
int32 for flags and counts.


Compression
Snappy by default. zstd is acceptable for archival.


Read in R
arrow::read_parquet()

polars.read_parquet() or pyarrow.parquet.read_table()

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
H.2 2.2 Partitioning
Partitioning splits a large dataset into a folder tree so queries only read the relevant subset of files. A partitioned Parquet dataset is a directory, not a single file. Each level of the tree is a partition key.
The standard partition scheme for hydrometric time series is:






supplier / data_type / gaugeID / year / <files>.parquet





For example, all Environment Agency flow records from 2024 sit in ea/Q/2001/2024/. A query asking for 2024 data never opens any other year folder. Without partitioning, the same query scans the entire dataset.
Partition keys should reflect the most common query patterns. Do not over-partition: very small files (under around 50 MB uncompressed) indicate too many partition levels.

Isolates data by source organisation

Allows reading only the variable needed

Allows reading only the variable needed

2023, 2024, 2025
Limits time range scanned for historical queries

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
section: I.1 3.1 What Delta adds over plain Parquet
text:
I.1 3.1 What Delta adds over plain Parquet
Plain Parquet files are immutable: once written they cannot be updated in place. Delta solves this by maintaining a transaction log alongside the Parquet data files. Every write, update, or delete is recorded in the log.

Rows can be updated or deleted without rewriting the entire dataset.
Concurrent reads and writes are handled safely (ACID transactions).
Schema changes are enforced and logged. A tool cannot accidentally write a column with the wrong type.
Time travel: you can query the table as it was at any earlier point, supporting auditability and debugging.

Delta tables must not be used outside DASH. They require the Databricks runtime to manage the transaction log correctly. When sharing data extracted from DASH, export as plain Parquet. The receiving tool does not need to know it came from a Delta table.

text:
L.1 6.1 What it is
A NetCDF file stores arrays with named dimensions, typically latitude, longitude, and time. Each variable (for example, precipitation or temperature) is stored as an array indexed by those dimensions. The file is self-describing: dimensions, coordinate values, and units are embedded inside the file rather than in a separate metadata document.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
section: L.2 6.2 Alternatives for gridded weather data
text:
L.2 6.2 Alternatives for gridded weather data
NetCDF is well-established and remains the required format for gridded outputs. For new workflows, two alternatives are worth knowing about.

L.2.1 Zarr
Zarr stores arrays in chunks as individual files or objects in cloud storage. Unlike NetCDF, which is a single file, Zarr is designed for parallel read and write in cloud environments. If the team moves gridded data to cloud object storage, Zarr is more efficient than NetCDF for large datasets accessed by many concurrent jobs. It is readable by xarray with a simple backend swap (xr.open_zarr()). Zarr is not yet the team standard: discuss with the Delegated Steward before adopting it in any Tier 1 workflow.


L.2.2 Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF (COG)
For single time-step rasters, for example a rainfall accumulation map for one event, a Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF may be more convenient than NetCDF. COGs are standard GeoTIFFs with internal tiling and overviews, allowing partial reads by any GIS tool without downloading the whole file. Use COG for raster deliverables to stakeholders or for display in GIS. Use NetCDF or Zarr for time-series raster data processed in code.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
M.1 7.1 Shapefiles
A shapefile is not a single file. It is at minimum three files sharing the same base name: .shp (geometry), .dbf (attributes), and .shx (spatial index). In practice there are usually more, including a .prj for the coordinate reference system and a .cpg for character encoding.
Shapefiles are the legacy standard for vector spatial data and are readable by nearly every GIS tool. However, they have well-known limitations that make them a poor choice for internal workflows.

Attribute column names are capped at ten characters.
File size is limited to 2 GB per component file.
No native support for timezone-aware timestamps or complex data types.
The format requires multiple files to be kept together, which creates risk in file transfers and version control.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
M.2 7.2 GeoParquet
GeoParquet is Parquet with a geometry column added according to a defined encoding standard. Geometry is stored as Well-Known Binary (WKB) within a standard Parquet column. The coordinate reference system and geometry type are recorded in the Parquet file metadata.
Because GeoParquet is Parquet, it inherits all the same advantages: columnar reads, strong typing, Snappy compression, and cross-tool compatibility. A spatial query that only needs geometry and one attribute column does not load the rest of the file from disk.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
M.3 7.3 Which to use
GeoParquet is the preferred format for vector spatial data stored and processed within team workflows. It is smaller, faster to query, and avoids the multi-file management problem of shapefiles.
Shapefiles remain acceptable in two situations: sharing data with an external party who requires shapefile format and receiving data from a supplier in shapefile format (retain as Bronze; convert to GeoParquet at Silver). Do not use shapefiles as the working format in any new pipeline.






GDAL 3.5 and above reads and writes GeoParquet natively. QGIS 3.28 and above supports GeoParquet. If a tool cannot open a .parquet file with geometry, check the GDAL version before considering a format change.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
N.1 8.1 Permitted uses

Sharing small datasets (under approximately 10,000 rows) with external parties who cannot read Parquet.
One-off data requests from stakeholders where Parquet is not practical.
Ingest of supplier-provided Bronze data where the supplier delivers CSV (retain as-is alongside converted Bronze Parquet).

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
N.2 8.2 Limitations and common misuse






CSV must not be used as a substitute for Parquet at any pipeline stage. It must not be used as the format for Bronze, Silver, or Gold tier datasets.





CSV has no type information. Every value is a string until something interprets it. This means:

Timestamps are stored as strings and may be read back in a different format by a different tool or locale.
Float precision is limited by the number of decimal places written. Silent rounding errors are possible.
There is no standard for representing null or missing values. Different tools use empty string, NA, NaN, NULL, or -9999 interchangeably, and none of these are enforced.
There is no schema. A column added or removed silently breaks downstream code with no error until the data is actually used.
Large CSV files are slow to read because every value must be parsed from text. Parquet columnar reads are typically 10-100x faster for the same data.

When writing CSV is necessary, use data.table::fwrite() in R or polars df.write_csv() in Python. Avoid using base R write.csv() or pandas df.to_csv() without specifying encoding explicitly.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
O.1 9.1 Permitted uses

Formal outputs and reports delivered to stakeholders who require Excel.
The Hydrometric Data Register (maintained as an Excel workbook on the file store, or as a Delta table in DASH).
Configuration tables or lookup tables that non-technical stakeholders need to edit.

title: Appendix E — File Format Reference
text:
O.2 9.2 Limitations and common misuse






Excel must not be used at any stage of a data or model pipeline. It must not be used to transfer data between tools, store intermediate results, or share datasets between team members.





Excel is a presentation and calculation tool, not a data storage format. Its use in analytical pipelines creates the following risks.

Dates are stored as numeric serial values interpreted differently across platforms and regions. Silent date conversion errors are common.
Numbers displayed with two decimal places may have their precision silently rounded if the cell format is changed.
There is no schema enforcement. A column can change type, be renamed, or be deleted and downstream code will fail silently or produce wrong results.
Excel will silently autocorrect values it recognises such as names, dates, long numeric strings (such as gauge IDs), and fractions are all known to be altered on open. This is not recoverable once saved.
Files over around 100,000 rows become slow and unstable. Excel has a hard row limit of 1,048,576 rows, which will silently truncate larger datasets.
Excel files are not suited to version control. Diff tools cannot show what changed between two versions of a .xlsx file.

When producing an Excel deliverable from pipeline data, generate it programmatically from a Parquet source using openxlsx2 in R or openpyxl in Python. Do not manually copy data into Excel from another tool.






If you receive data from an external party as an Excel file, convert it to Parquet as the first step and store the original .xlsx in Bronze unchanged. Never use the .xlsx directly as input to a model or analysis tool.
